title: Strategic Thinking Skills
blurb: How the best strategic minds in history, from Sun Tzu to Steve Jobs, think, and how to turn their tools (SWOT, blue ocean, game theory, scenarios) into habits.

lectures.title: The World of Strategic Thinking
lectures.hook: Strategy is the plan plus the ability to change the play in the seconds before the snap.

sections.html:
Ridgley opens with American football. The huddle calls a play based on the situation: distance to a first down, downs left, distance to score. The defense reads the same situation and calls its own play. The interesting part happens in the 10 to 15 seconds between breaking the huddle and the snap: the quarterback reads the defense and may change the play.

That moment is the course's definition of real strategy: a plan, plus a live loop of action and reaction against an opponent who is also thinking. A plan that can't adapt is just a schedule.

Strategic thinking is a cultivated skill, not a talent you are born with. Most people default to cognitive confinement: running routines they never question and avoiding thinking about tomorrow. Einstein's line about insanity (doing the same thing and expecting different results) is the opposite of strategic thinking.

Strategic thinking is different from daydreaming about the future. It means setting goals, building long-range plans from careful analysis of the internal and external environment, and letting where you want to be in five years decide what you do today.

Peter Drucker split thinking into two kinds. Thinking about objects (static planning) is easy because the variables barely move. Thinking about people is hard because you have to anticipate the moves and countermoves of competitors.

sections.h: The core vocabulary and its founders
sections.html:
• Strategic intent: the big idea a strategy serves (the career, the house, the market you want). It is what pulls your thinking toward the future.
  • Strategy: more than a plan. A way of seeing the future with your goals in mind, responding to a changing environment and, where possible, changing that environment in your favor.
  • Sun Tzu saw reality as fluid: the strategist must keep adapting.
  • Jomini contributed interior lines of communication and the concentration of force.
  • Clausewitz called uncertainty, chance and probability "friction," and answered it with coup d'oeil: a rapid, accurate stroke of intuition.
  • Liddell Hart argued for the indirect approach: never grind against an entrenched enemy's front; find another route.
  • Michael Porter brought it into business: strategy is "choosing a different set of activities to deliver a unique mix of value." In short, doing things differently. That one idea links Hannibal at Cannae (216 B.C.) and Apple in the 1980s.

Strategy is the higher-level plan; tactics are how you execute it. If your strategy is to become a doctor, med school courses are part of the strategy, and how you study for them are tactics. Clausewitz: tactics is using forces in battle; strategy is using battles to win the war.

The trap is thinking strategy can be separated from tactics. Many great plans die in execution. Good strategy is dynamic, adaptive and opportunistic, and depends on swift, bold, decisive tactics.

sections.h: Intelligence, surprise and a working definition
sections.html:
Intelligence and analysis are the raw material for strategy. You want to learn what the other side is doing and mislead them about what you are doing, as the U.S. did with the feigned amphibious invasion of Kuwait in 1991. Ridgley previews the five types of surprise: intention, time, place, strength and style, and tools like SWOT.

His robust definition: strategy is a method or plan to bring about a desired future (a goal reached or a problem solved) that assesses, acquires and allocates resources to their most effective use, and that anticipates competitor responses.

Strategic thinking is goal-directed, structured, future-focused, analytical, ambitious and instrumental: a resource like money or time.

takeaways: Real strategy = plan + live adaptation to an opponent who also adapts (the quarterback before the snap).
Strategic thinking is a trained skill; the default human mode is unquestioned routine.
Porter: strategy is doing things differently, choosing a different set of activities.
Strategy and tactics can't be separated; execution is where most plans fail.
A full definition covers the goal, resource allocation and anticipated competitor responses.

terms.def: The big, motivating idea a strategy exists to serve; it pulls planning toward a desired future.
Static thinking: living in routines you never question and refusing to think about tomorrow.
Clausewitz's 'glance of the eye': a rapid, accurate intuitive judgment in the middle of uncertainty.
Clausewitz's name for the uncertainty, chance and probability that make up most of conflict.
Harvard strategist; defined strategy as choosing a different set of activities to deliver a unique mix of value.
Management thinker who contrasted easy thinking about objects with hard thinking about people.

quiz.q: In the quarterback example, what marks 'genuine strategy'?
options: Calling the perfect play in the huddle
Changing the play after reading the defense
Running the same play until it works
quiz.why: The point is the action-reaction loop: the ability to change the plan based on what the opponent shows.

quiz.q: Porter's definition of strategy is best summarized as:
options: Doing the same things more efficiently
quiz.why: Porter: choosing a different set of activities to deliver a unique mix of value.

quiz.q: According to the lecture, strategic thinking is mostly an inborn talent.
quiz.why: It is a skill that must be cultivated and practiced.

quiz.q: Drucker said strategic thinking is harder than static thinking because it involves:
options: Thinking about people who react to you
quiz.why: Thinking about objects is easy; anticipating the actions and reactions of people is hard.

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of the five types of surprise?
quiz.why: The five are intention, time, place, strength and style.

quiz.q: Clausewitz described strategy as the employment of battles to achieve the object of war.
quiz.why: Tactics uses forces in battle; strategy uses battles toward the war's aim.

case.title: The gym that wants a 'strategy'
case.scenario: A neighborhood gym owner tells you: "Our strategy for next year is to be more efficient. We'll install a new booking app, adopt the same class schedule as the big chain across the street, and run a 10% discount in January." A new boutique studio opened two blocks away last month, and the chain just cut its prices.

questions.q: Is what the owner described a strategy in the sense of this lecture? Explain using at least two ideas from the lecture.
questions.model: Mostly no. It is a list of efficiency moves and imitation, not strategy. Porter's test is doing things differently, but copying the chain's schedule is the opposite. There is no strategic intent (what is the gym for, for whom?), no allocation of resources toward a distinctive goal, and no anticipation of competitor responses: the chain can match a 10% discount instantly, and the boutique studio is ignored. It is static thinking about objects (an app, a schedule) rather than thinking about people who will react.

questions.q: Sketch what a 'quarterback' version would include: a plan plus how it adapts to competitors' moves.
questions.model: A clear intent (e.g. the gym for over-40 beginners who are intimidated by chains), a few activities the chain and boutique don't do, and planned reads: if the chain cuts prices again, don't follow (price war); if the boutique copies our niche classes, shift to coaching packages. Set signals to watch (membership churn, competitor promotions) and decide in advance when you will change the play.

apply: Name one program or process in your life or work that calls itself 'strategy' but is really an efficiency tool. What would genuine strategy look like instead?
Watch the next sports match you see for the moment between play call and execution. Who adjusts, and based on what?

lectures.title: The Origins and Relevance of Ancient Strategy
lectures.hook: Six ancient minds, six portable lessons: power, innovation, fluid plans, knowing your opponent, reserves, and boldness.

sections.html:
Thucydides, an Athenian general (strategos) in the Peloponnesian War, wrote its history down to 411 B.C. The book founded international relations and the school of political realism. In the Melian dialogue, Athens tells the islanders of Melos that superior force is the only argument that matters, sweeping aside fairness, justice and the gods.

Lesson: some arenas really are governed by raw power (realpolitik). Recognize when you are in one, and ask how to use your advantages for an overwhelming win, or how to avoid being the Melians.

sections.h: Pagondas at Delium: innovation tips an even fight
sections.html:
At Delium (424 B.C.) the obscure Theban general Pagondas did several new things. He pursued the retreating Athenians rather than let them go, an early form of forward defense and preemption (striking a long-term threat, not just an immediate one). He held fresh cavalry in reserve and committed it at the decisive moment, the first recorded use of deliberate reserves joining an attack. He watched from a distance rather than fighting at the front, and modified his troop formation.

Delium counts as the birthplace of Western tactics. Lesson: surprise innovations can turn an evenly matched struggle.

sections.h: Sun Tzu: all plans are temporary
sections.html: The Art of War (5th century B.C., likely expanded later) rests on the fluid nature of reality. A plan can be obsolete the moment it is made. How you position yourself depends on two things: objective conditions in the physical environment and the subjective beliefs of competitors in it. The best plans emerge in the dynamic of action and response, guided by sound judgment and principles.

sections.h: Hannibal at Cannae: outsmart the stronger side
sections.html:
In 216 B.C. Hannibal, outnumbered in Rome's own territory, beat the Romans by turning their habits against them. The Romans formed a narrow, deep phalanx, which cancelled their numbers. Roman training told soldiers to chase a fleeing enemy, so when Hannibal's center appeared to give way, they pushed in and exposed their flanks. His cavalry drove off the Roman horse and, instead of chasing it, hit the Roman infantry from behind. Complete envelopment.

Lesson: against a stronger competitor, use what you know of their habits and weaknesses, especially when they feel most confident.

sections.h: Vegetius and Machiavelli: preparation and fortune
sections.html:
Vegetius (late 4th century A.D.) wrote the Epitoma rei militaris, the most popular military handbook for over 1,000 years. It looks mundane (recruiting, training, discipline), but it links to high strategy: strategy has three elements, intentions, capabilities and resources, and preparation builds capability. He stressed strategic reserves.

Machiavelli (The Prince; The Art of War) offers virtu (flexibility, foresight, energy, ability, political acumen: a developable skill) and fortuna, which he saw as malevolent and to be "beaten and mauled" into submission. Today we'd call that a bias toward action. Virtu meeting fortuna is an early version of emergent strategy.

sections.h: The five lessons of the past
sections.html:
1. Any field, however mindless, can be transformed by tactics: use special forces at special times in special ways.
  2. Plans must change; the best ones emerge from action and response.
  3. Preparation is the heart of capability. No reserves, no strategy.
  4. Know your opponents: surprise plus superb execution can beat a force twice your size.
  5. Be bold and seize your fortune; the hardest part is starting.

takeaways: Thucydides/Melian dialogue: some arenas run on raw power (realism).
Pagondas: reserves and innovation decide even fights; first deliberate reserves at Delium.
Sun Tzu: plans are temporary; position by terrain AND opponents' beliefs.
Hannibal: exploit the stronger side's habits (Cannae envelopment).
Vegetius: preparation builds capability; Machiavelli: virtu vs. fortuna, bias toward action.

terms.def: Passage in Thucydides where Athens tells Melos that superior force alone decides; the archetype of power politics.
School of thought (rooted in Thucydides) that sees international outcomes as driven by configurations of power.
Striking an enemy that poses a long-term threat before it becomes an immediate one.
Resources deliberately held back to be committed at a decisive moment.
Machiavelli's pair: developable qualities like foresight and energy (virtu) versus unpredictable, hostile fortune (fortuna).
Theban general at Delium (424 B.C.), credited with founding battlefield tactics, including the first deliberate use of reserves.
Carthaginian general who enveloped a larger Roman army at Cannae in 216 B.C.
Late Roman author of the Epitoma rei militaris, the handbook on training, discipline and reserves.

quiz.q: What tactical first is credited to Pagondas at Delium?
quiz.why: He held fresh cavalry in reserve and committed it at the crucial moment.

quiz.q: Why did the Romans' own training help Hannibal at Cannae?
options: They were trained to retreat early
They were trained to pursue a fleeing enemy
quiz.why: When his center seemed to withdraw, the Romans pressed forward and exposed their flanks.

quiz.q: Sun Tzu held that a well-made plan should be followed regardless of changing conditions.
quiz.why: For Sun Tzu all plans are temporary; the best ones spring from action and response.

quiz.q: Vegetius ties his 'pedestrian' topics to strategy through which three elements?
quiz.why: Preparation develops the capabilities that let intentions be achieved with available resources.

quiz.q: Machiavelli's advice to 'beat and maul' fortune is closest to:
quiz.why: He saw fortune as hostile and urged active, energetic response.

quiz.q: Ridgley's summary: 'If you have no reserves, you have no strategy.'
quiz.why: Reserves make maneuver possible; they come from training, discipline and planning.

case.title: The small agency vs. the giant
case.scenario: A 12-person design agency is pitching against a global agency with 20 times its staff for a regional bank's rebrand. Everyone knows the big agency's habit: it always sends its most senior partners to the first pitch, then hands the work to junior teams, and it reuses a standard 'brand discovery' template. The small agency has one founder who has personally led three bank rebrands and a modest cash buffer it has been saving.

questions.q: Which ancient lesson(s) apply here, and how would you use them?
questions.model: Hannibal's: exploit the stronger competitor's habits when it feels confident. Make the big agency's habit the issue: promise (in writing) that the people in the pitch room do the work, and show a discovery process built for this bank rather than a template. Pagondas/Vegetius on reserves: use the saved cash as a reserve committed at the decisive point, e.g. funding a free mini-prototype for the final round instead of spreading it thin.

questions.q: What is the risk of the Melian dialogue in this situation, and how do you avoid being the Melians?
questions.model: If the fight is purely about scale (global coverage, huge budgets), power decides and the small agency loses. Avoid fighting on that ground: don't argue you are 'just as big'; shift the decision criteria to things where size is a weakness (attention, senior involvement, speed).

apply: Where in your life is power the only real arbiter? What would you advise yourself if you were the Athenians, and if you were the Melians?
List areas where you have uncommonly strong reserves (skills, money, contacts, time). How could you hold some back and commit them at a decisive moment?
Think back to an unexpected situation that overwhelmed you. What virtu (trait) would have helped?

lectures.title: The Dawn of Modern Strategic Thinking
lectures.hook: Napoleon, Jomini and Clausewitz: why a checklist is the most dangerous thing a strategist can carry.

sections.html: The Enlightenment applied reason to everything, war included. Maurice de Saxe revived Vegetius; Frederick the Great mastered drilling large armies. With new ideas, new technology and growing populations, Napoleon (era roughly 1790 to 1815) arrived as a "perfect storm." He shows the power of ideas over material resources.

His Military Maxims remain a practical guide. Two warnings matter most. "Unhappy the general who comes on the field of battle with a system." Treating strategy as a formula is the biggest danger for modern strategists. And: theory is fine for general principles, but applying them is always dangerous. The best plan can be overturned by its own implementation, so keep flexibility and respond to the opponent.

• Central position (when outnumbered): drive a wedge between allied enemy armies, leave a small masking force to hold one, and fight the other with superior local force. This is concentration in time and space: be stronger at the point of attack even if weaker overall.
  • Indirect approach (when roughly equal and with room to maneuver): a small force feints at the enemy's front (a "demonstration") while the main force swings onto the flank or rear, onto the enemy's lines of communication and supply, forcing it to fight at a disadvantage or withdraw.

Jomini (Swiss officer in Napoleon's army) was first to separate strategy, tactics and logistics. His master principle was concentration at the decisive point, in four parts: bring most forces to bear on decisive areas and enemy communications without exposing your own; maneuver your major forces against only parts of the enemy; tactically mass on the decisive area of the battlefield; and get those forces into action fast. He also defined 12 geometric orders of battle.

Clausewitz (Prussian; On War, published posthumously by his widow Marie) placed war in a political context. War is a function of violence, chance and political aims. Chance matters most to us: the commander's courage and skill against uncertainty, resolved through coup d'oeil. Militaries now accept that intuitive decision-making can be taught.

Jomini dominated the 19th century. In the American Civil War, commanders treating him as a checklist launched massed frontal assaults into rifles and minié balls. The fault was the checklist mindset, not Jomini. Creative exceptions: Stonewall Jackson ("mystify, mislead, and surprise"; Shenandoah 1862) and Nathan Bedford Forrest ("Get there first with the most"; Brice's Crossroads 1864). Guderian's panzers in 1940 applied the same idea of overwhelming force at one point.

World War I generals tried to concentrate like Jomini but missed that technology had shifted the advantage to the defense. Liddell Hart responded with his indirect approach built around the tank. In the 1930s, geopolitics and geographical determinism appeared; Mackinder's 1904 formula: who rules Eastern Europe commands the Heartland; who rules the Heartland commands the World Island; who rules the World Island commands the World.

Keep two tools: the indirect approach and the central position. And notice the frontal assault is used far too often.

takeaways: Napoleon: never bring a system to the battlefield; principles must flex in execution.
Central position (outnumbered) = wedge + mask + local superiority; indirect approach (equal) = feint front, hit flank/rear.
Jomini: strategy/tactics/logistics; concentration at the decisive point.
Clausewitz: violence, chance, political aims; coup d'oeil beats chance.
Checklist strategy produced the Civil War and WWI slaughters.

terms.def: Napoleon's move when outnumbered: split allied enemies, mask one, and defeat the other with local superiority.
Feint at the enemy's front while the main force strikes its flank, rear or supply lines; avoid head-on attacks on strength.
Massing superior strength at the decisive point and time, even when outnumbered overall.
Systematic thinking about how geography shapes politics and conflict; criticized as geographic determinism.
Swiss theorist who separated strategy, tactics and logistics and made concentration the core principle.
Prussian theorist (On War): war as violence, chance and politics; coup d'oeil.
Geographer whose 1904 Heartland formula founded geopolitics.

quiz.q: When outnumbered by two allied armies, Napoleon typically used:
quiz.why: He drove a wedge between them and fought one with local superiority while masking the other.

quiz.q: Napoleon said: 'Unhappy the general who comes on the field of battle with a system.'
quiz.why: His warning against treating strategy as a formula.

quiz.q: Jomini is credited with being first to distinguish:
quiz.why: His Art of War defined these as three distinct realms.

quiz.q: Clausewitz's three variables of conflict are:
quiz.why: The strategist balances violence, chance and political aims.

quiz.q: Why did massed frontal assaults fail so badly in the Civil War and WWI?
options: Technology had shifted the advantage to the defense
quiz.why: Rifles, minié balls and later machine guns made frontal attacks nearly suicidal; commanders followed checklists.

quiz.q: Forrest's 'Get there first with the most' is an expression of Jomini's principle of concentration.
quiz.why: It packs surprise, speed, objective and mass into one phrase; Brice's Crossroads showed concentration at work.

case.title: Two rivals at once
case.scenario: You run a small food-delivery startup in one city. Two larger competitors have just announced a partnership: one will cover restaurants, the other groceries, and they'll cross-promote. Together they outspend you 5 to 1, but each is only strong in its own category, and their integration won't be complete for six months.

questions.q: Which Napoleonic strategy fits this situation, and how would you apply it?
questions.model: The central position: you face two allied opponents and are outnumbered overall. Drive a wedge in the gap before integration is complete. Concentrate nearly everything on one front (say, grocery delivery in the neighborhoods where the grocery partner is weakest) to win local superiority, while a small 'masking force' (basic retention offers) holds your position against the other. Time matters: act inside the six-month window.

questions.q: What would the checklist-minded (bad Jomini) version look like, and why would it fail?
questions.model: Matching both rivals everywhere at once with discounts and ads: a frontal assault on two entrenched fronts with one-fifth the resources. It spreads your force thin, ignores the timing window and the gap between allies, and fights on the ground where they are strongest.

apply: Is there a situation where two or more parties are teaming up against you? How could you concentrate against only one part of the opposition?
Identify an oblique approach you could use against a competitor: where would you 'demonstrate,' and where would you really strike?
Recall a time a hunch solved a problem. Where did it come from, and how could you listen to it more?

lectures.title: Modern Principles of Strategic Conflict
lectures.hook: Nine principles that survived every change in weapons, from 1940's Ardennes to your next negotiation.

sections.html: The French trusted the Maginot Line and assumed the dense Ardennes forest would stop an attack. The Germans went through the Ardennes, achieving rare strategic surprise. They combined two ideas: assembling activities in innovative ways (tanks, aircraft and infantry together: blitzkrieg) and the indirect approach. They used offensive, mass, maneuver, economy of force and surprise. A sound principle is one that keeps working as technology, place and players change.

sections.h: The nine principles (Fuller, adopted by the U.S. military)
sections.html:
• Objective: aim every operation at a clear, decisive, attainable goal.
  • Offensive: seize, retain and exploit the initiative.
  • Mass: concentrate overwhelming effect at the decisive place and time.
  • Economy of force: allocate only the minimum to secondary efforts.
  • Maneuver: put the enemy at a disadvantage through flexible use of power.
  • Unity of command: one commander and one effort per objective.
  • Security: never let the enemy gain unexpected advantage.
  • Surprise: strike at a time, place or manner they're unprepared for.
  • Simplicity: clear, uncomplicated plans and concise orders.

Fuller grouped them under control, pressure and resistance.

Everyone involved must know the objective, and every intermediate step must contribute to it directly, quickly and economically. Too many people confuse tactics with the goal; even Robert E. Lee is faulted as a master tactician but a mediocre strategist. The army's METT-T framework (mission, enemy, troops, terrain, time) translates easily: competitor, your people and energy, your organizational landscape.

Offensive action seizes the initiative and forces opponents to react. Defense is a temporary necessity before resuming the offensive.

sections.h: Mass, economy of force and maneuver
sections.html:
Mass is synchronizing power in concentrated time and space, and sustaining it. It's harder than it sounds in big organizations. Because mass is never unlimited, economy of force matters: everything gets a job, and secondary efforts get the minimum so you can mass at the decisive point. In business, don't squander resources on peripheral ventures.

Maneuver is moving relative to the opponent for positional advantage. It keeps them off balance, lets you choose where and when to fight (or decline to), and makes you unpredictable. It needs agility of thought, plans and organization.

Unity of command means one person with authority; when that's impossible (partners, alliances), aim for unity of effort: coordination toward a shared objective. Diffused responsibility and closed-door decisions undermine both.

Security means protecting your plans, resources and people by understanding competitors' likely courses of action. Surprise is a force multiplier, achieved through speed, intelligence, deception, unexpected force, operational security and varied methods. Simplicity ties it together: simple plans get executed; complex ones confuse.

takeaways: A principle is sound if it holds across eras and technologies.
Nine principles: objective, offensive, mass, economy of force, maneuver, unity of command, security, surprise, simplicity.
Fuller's grouping: control, pressure, resistance.
METT-T is a portable planning checklist: mission, enemy, troops, terrain, time.
Don't confuse tactical brilliance with strategic progress.

terms.def: Germany's 'lightning war' combining tanks, aircraft and infantry with the indirect approach (France, 1940).
Giving secondary efforts only the minimum so that maximum strength can be massed at the decisive point.
Coordination of separate actors toward a shared objective when single command isn't possible.
Army planning framework: mission, enemy, troops, terrain, time available.
British colonel who distilled the principles of war during WWI; adopted by the U.S. Army.

quiz.q: Which principle says to give secondary efforts only the minimum necessary?
quiz.why: Economy of force frees resources to mass at the decisive point.

quiz.q: Fuller grouped the nine principles under:
quiz.why: Fuller's three headings.

quiz.q: In 1940 the Germans attacked the Maginot Line head-on and broke through.
quiz.why: They went through the Ardennes, around the line: strategic surprise plus the indirect approach.

quiz.q: When unity of command is impossible (e.g., an alliance), the course says aim for:
quiz.why: Unity of effort: coordination and cooperation toward a commonly recognized objective.

quiz.q: What does the 'T' that appears twice in METT-T stand for?
quiz.why: Mission, enemy, troops, terrain, time available.

quiz.q: According to the offensive principle, defense should be a temporary respite before regaining the initiative.
quiz.why: The side that keeps the initiative forces others to react.

case.title: The product launch with nine priorities
case.scenario: A mid-size software company is launching a new product. The plan has nine 'equal priority' goals, four executives co-own the launch with no final decision-maker, the marketing budget is split evenly across eight countries, and the launch date was announced publicly a year in advance with a full feature list.

questions.q: Identify at least four principles of war the plan violates and explain each.
questions.model: Objective: nine equal priorities means no decisive objective. Unity of command: four co-owners, no one with authority. Mass and economy of force: an even split across eight countries means nowhere gets overwhelming effect. Security and surprise: announcing date and features a year ahead lets competitors prepare. Simplicity is also violated by the tangle of goals and owners.

questions.q: Propose a revised plan that applies the principles.
questions.model: One objective (e.g. 1,000 paying customers in the two best-fit markets within 90 days); one accountable launch owner; mass 70% of budget on those two markets, minimal holding effort elsewhere (economy of force); keep exact features and timing quiet until close to launch (security, surprise); a one-page plan everyone can repeat (simplicity).

apply: Do an 'idea inventory': which of your beliefs about how the world works were formed in conditions that no longer exist (like France's WWI-based thinking)?
Pick three principles and check whether someone has used them against you recently.
Pick three principles and apply them to a current goal.

lectures.title: Geography—Know Your Terrain
lectures.hook: Every battlefield, from a chessboard to a conference room, has positional power. Map it before you fight on it.

sections.html: Geopolitics studies how unchanging physical geography conditions politics and conflict. It's criticized as geographic determinism (a single-factor explanation) and was tainted by Nazi use, but its core idea survives: geography is a source of political, military and economic power. Spykman: geography is the most fundamental factor in foreign policy because it is the most permanent; "ministers come and ministers go... but mountain ranges stand unperturbed." Small features matter too, like the sunken road of Ohain that wrecked Napoleon's cavalry at Waterloo.

Geography matters only as people use it for a purpose, and its value is usually temporary. Competition is a three-way dialectic: opponents maneuver against each other while interacting with the terrain. The rules of the contest create the terrain's power: move the goal in football and every position's value changes.

Two kinds of power: potential positional power (from the technology and tactics both sides could invest in the field) and realized positional power (from actual deployment, condition, numbers, skill and timing).

sections.h: Chess, conference rooms and boxing rings
sections.html: In chess the four center squares have the highest potential power, but every move changes each square's value, and pieces and squares amplify each other (synergy). A conference room works the same way: seating, table shape and chairs create power configurations. Negotiators manipulate micro-geography, as at P'anmunjŏm. In boxing, a featureless ring still gives each square foot meaning relative to the fighters.

The military's systematic method for understanding the ground, easily adapted to business and personal decisions:

  1. Define the battlefield environment: what influences both sides; its limits; what's unknown but should be known.
  2. Describe the battlefield's effects: terrain and weather, plus infrastructure, politics, press, population, demographics.
  3. Evaluate the competitor: how it normally organizes and operates (from history and threat models).
  4. Determine the competitor's possible courses of action: given its preferences and this environment, what will it likely try?

The Soviets learned through intelligence exactly when and where the Germans would attack the Kursk bulge (120 miles wide, 90 deep) with a pincer. Over months they built successive defense lines, used terrain to channel the Germans into minefields, artillery zones and hidden antitank points, and ground down the entire German strategic tank reserve in a week. The initiative passed to the Soviets for good.

Lesson: if you know where you'll be attacked, prepare the ground; once a challenger commits, wear them down with successive lines on terrain you chose. Choose your ground beforehand whenever possible.

takeaways: Geography is power, but only relative to how people use it and to the rules.
Potential vs. realized positional power.
Micro-geography (seating, venues) shapes negotiations.
IPB: define environment, describe effects, evaluate competitor, determine their courses of action.
Kursk: known attack + prepared terrain = defense in depth.

terms.def: Criticism of geopolitics as explaining complex outcomes by geography alone.
Power a location could provide given the technology and tactics available to both sides.
Power actually produced by how, when and how well forces are deployed.
Four-step military method for analyzing the ground, its effects, the competitor and its likely courses of action.
Successive prepared lines that absorb and wear down an attacker on chosen terrain (Kursk 1943).
Geopolitical theorist, 'godfather of containment'; geography is the most permanent factor in foreign policy.

quiz.q: What is the final step of IPB?
options: Determine the competitor's possible courses of action
quiz.why: It ends by asking what the competitor will likely do, given its habits and this environment.

quiz.q: According to the lecture, geography has value in and of itself regardless of how people use it.
quiz.why: It takes importance only as people use it for a purpose, and its value is usually temporary.

quiz.q: Changing where the goal is in football illustrates that positional power depends on:
quiz.why: The rules create the terrain's positional power.

quiz.q: What did the Soviets do at Kursk?
options: Built successive prepared defense lines on chosen terrain
quiz.why: Defense in depth wore down the German tank reserve.

quiz.q: Realized positional power comes from actual deployment, condition, numbers and timing.
quiz.why: Potential power is about what could be invested; realized power is what is actually deployed.

quiz.q: In chess, which squares have the highest potential power at the start?
quiz.why: Early control of the center is the basis of a winning game, though values change every move.

case.title: The salary negotiation
case.scenario: You're negotiating a raise. Your manager has suggested meeting Friday at 5 p.m. in their office, sitting behind their desk. Budget decisions for next year are finalized the following Wednesday. You know your manager tends to agree to things that make them look good to their own boss, and dislikes surprises in front of others.

questions.q: Run a quick IPB on this negotiation.
questions.model: 1) Environment: the decision window closes Wednesday; the manager's boss and the budget process influence both sides; unknown: the size of the raise pool. 2) Effects: Friday 5 p.m. means tired and rushed; their office and desk give them positional power; after Wednesday the terrain disappears. 3) Competitor: wants to look good upward, avoids public surprises. 4) Likely courses: defer ('let's revisit next quarter'), offer a small standard raise, or agree if it can be framed as their win.

questions.q: How would you reshape the terrain in your favor?
questions.model: Move the meeting earlier in the week before Wednesday (time terrain), at a neutral spot like a small meeting room or side-by-side seating (micro-geography), and bring a one-page case framed as something your manager can take to their boss. Raise it privately so they aren't surprised in front of others.

apply: What factors give you a geographic advantage in your own interactions (where you sit, where you meet, whose turf)?
List the unwritten rules in a setting you compete in. Where is the gap between official and real rules, and does it give you room to maneuver?
If you had to defend against a strong opponent, what successive 'lines of defense' could you prepare?

lectures.title: Grand Strategists and Strategic Intent
lectures.hook: Without a big, clear intent, strategy is just soulless technique.

sections.html: In 1989 Gary Hamel and C. K. Prahalad named strategic intent in Harvard Business Review. They attacked the "strategy of imitation": copying techniques instead of having a strategy. Strategic intent creates an obsession to win: a long-term aspiration that reaches beyond current capabilities and forces you to build new resources. Tailoring ambition to current capability preserves the status quo; stretch goals without intent are a recipe for failure. Japanese firms (Honda, Matsushita, Sony, Toyota) used this after WWII: identify an extreme gap between resources and ambition, then close it.

Joseph Campbell's hero's journey (Prometheus, Ulysses, the Grail) is the archetype of intent overcoming impossible obstacles, and your own life has the same structure. Vince Lombardi: "Winning isn't everything, it's the only thing," translated into a mid-range goal every player could act on: "You never win a game unless you beat the guy in front of you." Seen as a value chain, every player's effort serves the intent. Nobody perfects blocking technique for "best practice."

• Kennedy: "We choose to go to the moon in this decade," achieved within ten years.
  • Martin Luther King Jr. joined a powerful vision (social justice) with a strategy every individual could execute: nonviolent civil disobedience. Against him stood George Wallace's own intent ("Segregation now... forever"). King won with intent and strategy alone; the Civil Rights Act of 1964 followed.
  • George Kennan's 1946 Long Telegram: the Soviets ignore reason but respond to force, so "contain" them. Containment guided U.S. policy for 40 years until 1989 to 1991.
  • Lincoln fought not reactively but to preserve the Union, articulated in the Gettysburg Address.

Ratan Tata (2003) demanded a four-seat "People's Car" for about $2,000, on a brutal timeline, over engineers' objections. The Tata Nano (2010) may have triggered a management revolution comparable to kanban and kaizen.

Failures: DEC (1992): "committed to providing high-quality products and services and being a leader in data processing." Vague, unfocused; swallowed by Compaq six years later. Levi Strauss under Bob Haas adopted an inward-looking vision unrelated to selling jeans; share fell from 48% to 17% (1990 to 2000). Imperial Japan's "Co-Prosperity Sphere" overreached: ambition without the capabilities to match.

Strategy without intent is "a great flurry of activity." Vague bold pronouncements aren't courage. Real intent needs boldness grounded in an accurate read of reality, and it closes off options on purpose to pursue one goal single-mindedly.

takeaways: Strategic intent = obsession to win + a deliberate gap between ambition and current resources.
Stretch goals need intent; intent needs translation into mid-range goals people can act on (Lombardi).
Good intent is concrete (moon in a decade, $2,000 car); bad intent is vague (DEC) or inward-looking (Levi's).
Ambition without capability-building becomes overreach (imperial Japan).
Real intent closes off options.

terms.def: Copying competitors' techniques as a substitute for strategy; what strategic intent was coined to counter.
A goal deliberately beyond current capabilities, forcing the development of new resources.
Joseph Campbell's archetypal story of a hero overcoming seemingly impossible obstacles.
Kennan's strategic intent: meet Soviet expansion with American power; U.S. policy for 40 years.
Strategy scholar who, with C. K. Prahalad, coined 'strategic intent' (1989).
Hamel's co-author; later known for 'bottom of the pyramid' market solutions to poverty.
Diplomat whose 1946 Long Telegram set the U.S. containment policy.

quiz.q: Hamel and Prahalad coined strategic intent to counter:
quiz.why: They saw firms pursuing imitative techniques as a substitute for strategy.

quiz.q: Setting stretch goals without strategic intent is, per the lecture, a recipe for failure.
quiz.why: Stretch goals need the animating intent behind them.

quiz.q: What made DEC's 1992 statement a failure of strategic intent?
quiz.why: 'High-quality products... leader in data processing' rallies no one and closes no options.

quiz.q: Lombardi translated 'winning' into which actionable goal?
options: Beat the guy in front of you
quiz.why: Intent must become mid-range goals each player can execute.

quiz.q: Imperial Japan's Co-Prosperity Sphere illustrates:
quiz.why: Japan didn't have the capabilities to match its ambitions.

quiz.q: According to the lecture, good strategic intent keeps all options open.
quiz.why: It deliberately closes off options to pursue one goal with single-minded fervor.

case.title: The nonprofit's new vision
case.scenario: A literacy nonprofit's board proposes a new vision statement: "We strive to be a leading, innovative organization committed to excellence in education and community impact." Currently it tutors 400 kids a year in one city with 15 staff. A board member privately says the real dream is that no child in the region leaves third grade unable to read.

questions.q: Evaluate the proposed statement against the lecture's criteria.
questions.model: It is DEC all over again: generic words ('leading', 'innovative', 'excellence') that any organization could use, nothing measurable, no stretch, no options closed, nothing a tutor or donor can act on. It inspires no obsession to win.

questions.q: Rewrite it as real strategic intent and give one Lombardi-style mid-range goal.
questions.model: Intent: "By 2032, no child in our region leaves third grade unable to read." That is concrete and far beyond 400 kids a year, which forces capability building (training volunteers, partnering with schools, a scalable curriculum). Mid-range goal: "Every tutor gets one child from below grade level to grade level each semester." It also closes options: drop the adult-literacy side programs that dilute focus.

apply: Can you state the strategic intent behind your biggest current goal in one or two sentences?
Are your goals easy to meet on purpose? Set one that seems out of reach, and list the resources and capabilities it would force you to build.
Spend a few minutes thinking 'grandly' about an idea most people would dismiss with 'you can't do that.'

lectures.title: The Core and the Rise of Strategic Planning
lectures.hook: Mission first, then a six-step loop. And beware the binder on the shelf.

sections.html:
The French Foreign Legion draws its identity from the stand at Camerone (Mexico, 1863) and the respect its enemies showed. Every organization should have a founding myth that captures its spirit (think Apple's two young men in a garage).

The myth feeds the mission statement, which anchors strategy and strategic intent. Good ones are bold and inspiring: Coca-Cola's "To refresh the world; to inspire moments of optimism and happiness..." Henry Mintzberg: the most interesting, successful companies "are not boring"; their strategies are novel, creative, sometimes playful. Equal Exchange ("Fairness to farmers...") shows how a mission can generate achievable objectives.

Planning began in the military: the Prussian general staff (1807) started formal staff planning. Business picked it up slowly: the Harvard policy model (1920s) was a call to action more than a method. After WWII, Ford hired ten former officers (the team led by Robert McNamara), introducing planning, control systems and fiscal discipline; McNamara later took planning to the Pentagon. By the 1960s planning was standard but had degenerated into an annual budgeting exercise built on last year's numbers. U.S. dominance hid the flaws until the 1970s, when Japanese competition and the oil states exposed them: the models ignored human irrationality and the moves of other players.

• Predetermination: believing we can predict the future ("predict and prepare").
  • Detachment: planners removed from the action; formulation cut off from implementation.
  • Formalization: the "binder mentality"; the plan ossifies on a shelf and drifts from what the company does.

McKinsey's 1978 "The Evolution of Strategic Management" described four phases: financial planning (1950s annual budgets), forecast-based planning, externally oriented planning, and finally strategic management, which welds planning and management into one process and spreads strategic thinking throughout the organization.

1. Mission: your reason for being; the core everything refers back to.
  2. Objectives: clear, concise, achievable, measurable goals that serve the mission.
  3. Situation analysis (environmental scan): external and internal environments. The most involved step.
  4. Strategy formulation: decide how to get from here to there; allocate resources; connect decisions to the people who implement.
  5. Implementation: where companies fail by not following the military dictum "supervise and refine."
  6. Control: a monitoring mechanism; when it signals trouble, loop back to the situation analysis.

Porter's reminders: strategy means doing things differently, and the right timeframe may be a decade or more. A single budget cycle is too short; long plans build unique capabilities and fit across activities.

takeaways: A founding myth feeds a mission; a mission anchors strategy.
Early planning degenerated into annual budgeting and ignored competitors and irrationality.
Mintzberg's fallacies: predetermination, detachment, formalization.
Six steps: mission, objectives, situation analysis, formulation, implementation, control (then loop).
Mission = reason for being; objectives = measurable goals that serve it.

terms.def: A concise statement of an organization's (or person's) reason for being that anchors strategy.
Mintzberg: the false belief that we can predict the future and plan for one line of events.
Mintzberg: planners removed from the action, separating formulation from implementation.
Mintzberg: the plan ossifies in a binder and drifts away from reality.
Military dictum for implementation: don't issue orders and assume they're executed.
Contrarian management scholar; critic of rigid strategic planning; 'successful companies are not boring.'
Led the ex-military team at Ford; brought formal planning to the Pentagon as Kennedy's defense secretary.

quiz.q: What is the correct order of the six-step process?
options: Objective, mission, strategy, analysis, control, implementation
Mission, objective, situation analysis, strategy formulation, implementation, control
Situation analysis, mission, objective, implementation, strategy, control
Mission, strategy formulation, objective, control, implementation, analysis
quiz.why: Mission, objective, situation analysis, formulation, implementation, control, then loop back.

quiz.q: The 'binder on the shelf' describes which fallacy?
quiz.why: Formalization: the plan ossifies and drifts from what the company actually does.

quiz.q: In McKinsey's 1978 scheme, the highest phase is forecast-based planning.
quiz.why: The highest is strategic management, which welds planning and management together.

quiz.q: When the control step signals trouble, you should loop back to:
quiz.why: Check whether environmental factors have changed.

quiz.q: According to Porter, the proper timeframe for strategic planning may be:
quiz.why: A single budget cycle is usually too short for a strategy to work.

quiz.q: A mission is the reason for being; objectives are the measurable goals set to fulfill it.
quiz.why: If your mission is to heal the sick, objectives might be degrees, residencies, a practice.

case.title: The café that plans by spreadsheet
case.scenario: A café owner does 'strategic planning' every December: take this year's revenue, add 8%, set the budget, put the document in a folder. Last year a chain opened nearby and foot traffic fell 20% by spring, but the plan wasn't revisited until the next December. The owner never wrote down what the café is for.

questions.q: Diagnose the problems using Mintzberg's fallacies and McKinsey's phases.
questions.model: It's stuck in McKinsey's first phase (financial planning as an annual budget). Predetermination: it assumes next year looks like this year plus 8%. Formalization: the plan sits in a folder and isn't consulted. There's no control step, so the chain's arrival didn't trigger a rethink for months. No mission means nothing anchors the objectives.

questions.q: Walk the owner through the six steps in a few lines each.
questions.model: Mission: e.g. "the neighborhood's living room for remote workers." Objectives: 60 regulars with a weekly pass by June; 25% of revenue from laptop-hours packages. Situation analysis: chain nearby (cheaper, faster), remote-worker growth, our strengths (space, quiet, owner knows names). Formulation: don't compete on speed; invest in seating, power, a quiet room. Implementation: owner checks in weekly, assigns tasks. Control: monthly review of regulars and revenue mix; if off-track, re-scan the environment.

apply: Do you have a personal mission statement? Write one now and ask honestly whether it inspires you.
Compare your employer's (or school's) mission statement with what it actually does. Measure the gap between slogan and action.
Sketch the six steps for one long-term personal goal.

lectures.title: Which Business Strategy? Fundamental Choices
lectures.hook: You compete either on low cost or on difference. If you can choose, choose difference.

sections.html: Following Porter, every competitor travels under one of two umbrellas: cost leadership or differentiation. Within them you can apply tactics, target segments or focus on parts of the value chain. Focus is the offshoot: serving a narrow segment, by cost or by difference.

Sell at the lowest price the market will bear and profit on volume, attracting value-conscious buyers. Walmart: volume, volume discounts, squeeze suppliers, pass savings on. In 2007 it drifted upmarket, dropped 300+ low-price items, alienated its base, and returned to the formula in 2011. Netflix (2011) raised prices and split streaming from mail and lost over a million subscribers in six months.

Commodities like cement almost force price competition: low margins, fierce rivalry. Many job seekers unknowingly choose low cost by presenting themselves as interchangeable commodities. A chiropractor who specializes in athletes' low back pain escapes commodity pricing.

Military parallel: WWI armies all competed on "low cost," producing undifferentiated, bloody stalemate until the tank broke it. In WWII Germany differentiated with elite divisions; the U.S. and USSR spread quality evenly and won on volume. That success convinced many postwar U.S. firms that low-price/high-volume was the only way.

Offer something unique and valuable beyond low price: a unique selling proposition (USP). The common error is blurring the proposition to "do more things" for more people until the brand means nothing. Rolex and Casio both sell watches but don't compete; the Tata Nano (under $3,000) and Lexus LS460 ($75,000) both sell cars. Differentiation means specializing, adding features, delivering crucial service superbly, and building a reputation or aura (Nike).

Military: the U.S. ended Cold War volume competition (ICBMs, bombers, subs) with the Strategic Defense Initiative (1983), using research and economic advantages the Soviets couldn't imitate.

Differentiating a commodity is the hardest trick. Starbucks differentiated coffee by how it's served: a European-style "lifestyle" destination. When it broadened its format (2007) it lost distinctiveness; Schultz returned in 2008 and refocused on the USP.

Focus is hyper-differentiation for a narrow market: ethnic grocers, ultra-high-end cars, Equal Exchange (fair-trade coffee for buyers motivated by social justice; small, stable, profitable niche), and Jolt Cola ("All the sugar, and twice the caffeine") targeting rebels against the health trend.

Inventory your resources and capabilities and check strategic fit with your intentions. Then write a personal USP: one sentence describing what you offer that few can match. Do it for a trusted friend too, and swap.

takeaways: Two generic strategies: cost leadership and differentiation; focus is an offshoot.
Low-cost players that drift from their formula get punished (Walmart 2007, Netflix 2011).
Commodity thinking traps people too: job seekers who sell themselves on 'price.'
Differentiation = USP; blurring it dilutes the brand (Starbucks 2007).
Check strategic fit and write a one-sentence personal USP.

terms.def: Competing by selling at the lowest price the market bears and profiting on volume.
Competing by offering something unique and valuable beyond low price.
Serving a narrow, sharply defined segment better than anyone, via cost or differentiation.
The distinctive value you offer that competitors can't easily match.
Alignment between your resources and capabilities and your intentions.

quiz.q: Rolex and Casio illustrate that:
options: Well-differentiated products may not compete at all
quiz.why: Each offers a different value; they serve different buyers.

quiz.q: Equal Exchange's fair-trade coffee is an example of:
quiz.why: A niche strategy targeting customers motivated by social justice.

quiz.q: Walmart's 2007 move upmarket strengthened its core strategy.
quiz.why: It alienated its base customers; Walmart returned to its formula in 2011.

quiz.q: How did Starbucks differentiate a commodity?
options: The way coffee is served: a lifestyle destination
quiz.why: A European-style coffee house experience.

quiz.q: Job seekers who present themselves like everyone else are, per Ridgley:
quiz.why: They advertise themselves as commodities and end up competing on price.

quiz.q: In WWI the tank was a differentiation move that broke an undifferentiated stalemate.
quiz.why: All sides had been competing 'on volume' until the tank.

case.title: The freelance translator
case.scenario: Mira is a freelance German-English translator on a platform with 4,000 other German-English translators. Clients filter by price, and she keeps lowering her rate to win jobs. She has a law degree, spent two years in a Swiss bank's compliance team, and loves writing.

questions.q: Which strategy is Mira currently following, and why is it a trap?
questions.model: Unwittingly, cost leadership: she's a commodity among 4,000 others competing on price, with low margins and endless rivalry. She can't win a price war against people with lower costs of living or machine translation.

questions.q: Write Mira a personal USP and say whether it's differentiation or focus.
questions.model: "I translate Swiss and German financial-compliance and legal documents into English that a regulator would sign off on, because I've worked inside a Swiss bank's compliance team." It's a focus strategy (narrow segment: finance/legal compliance, DACH region) built on genuine differentiation (law degree plus insider experience). She should leave the general platform and price on value, e.g. per project.

apply: How do you compete professionally: doing the same thing as everyone, faster, or combining a skill set no one else has? List the components.
When you hear Nike charges a premium, do you say 'it's not worth it' or 'what's the formula'? Apply the second question to yourself.
If you launched a coffee brand tomorrow, what mix of attributes, service, brand and distribution would set it apart?

lectures.title: Your Competitive Advantage—Find the Blue Ocean
lectures.hook: Stop fighting in the red ocean. Eliminate, reduce, raise, create.

sections.html: Madonna arrived in New York in 1977 unknown, and her 1983 debut seemed to come from nowhere. It didn't: she set a core mission and objectives, held relentless strategic intent, and carved out uncontested space with a USP and personal brand unlike anyone's. She didn't benchmark; she studied the competition coolly to find empty space.

Many think competition means doing the same thing better: benchmarking and best practices. Do only that and you play a game of mimicry. W. Chan Kim and Renée Mauborgne (INSEAD), in Blue Ocean Strategy, describe red oceans (competitors fighting over a shrinking profit pool, commodity margins) and blue oceans (uncontested market space created by differentiating in ways that matter to a target market).

sections.h: The value curve and the Four Actions Framework
sections.html:
A value curve plots how an offer performs across an industry's accepted factors of competition (for cars: price, prestige, mileage, size, comfort, performance, longevity, safety, service). The conventional model competes on all of them. The blue ocean approach questions the factors themselves:

  1. Eliminate: which factors the industry takes for granted should go?
  2. Reduce: which should drop well below the standard?
  3. Raise: which should rise well above it?
  4. Create: which should exist that the industry never offered?

Tata's Nano ignored most car factors and bet on price for the ignored bottom of the pyramid.

Wine competed on price, intriguing terminology, high-visibility marketing, aging quality, vineyard prestige, complexity and range. Casella Wines eliminated the jargon and complexity (even different bottles for red and white), reduced range (one red, one white at first), raised fun (a bright kangaroo label, lowercase name in brackets) and created easy drinking, ease of selection, and fun and adventure. It grew the market itself by attracting new wine drinkers and prospered during an industry dip, later adding a few offerings that reinforced the USP.

sections.h: Personal blue oceans and your brand
sections.html:
A résumé of experience and eagerness isn't a blue ocean. Ridgley's provocations: the manager blamed for the failed 1993 Diet Coke campaign (which cost Lintas the Coke account) could have owned it, becoming "the manager who lost the Coke account" and turning that into insight, a book, TV commentary. Or join BP at its 2010 low point and build a brand as part of the turnaround. Risky, but the point is to untrain conventional thinking and stop needing external validation; truly new ideas look odd at first.

You'll be labeled by others anyway, so take control. Your brand is your reputation: Mercedes means quality, Volvo means safety. What does your name mean?

takeaways: Benchmarking alone = mimicry in a red ocean.
Blue ocean = uncontested space created by redefining the factors of competition.
Four Actions: eliminate, reduce, raise, create; they redraw the value curve.
[yellow tail] grew the market by making wine simple and fun.
Your personal brand is your reputation; shape it before others do.

terms.def: A crowded market where competitors fight over a shrinking profit pool with commodity margins.
Uncontested market space created by differentiating in ways a target market values.
A plot of how an offer performs across an industry's accepted factors of competition.
Kim and Mauborgne's eliminate/reduce/raise/create questions for building a new value curve.
Your reputation: what people think first when they hear your name.
INSEAD professors W. Chan Kim and Renée Mauborgne, authors of Blue Ocean Strategy.

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of the Four Actions?
quiz.why: Eliminate, reduce, raise, create. Benchmarking is red-ocean behavior.

quiz.q: What did [yellow tail] create that the wine industry didn't offer?
quiz.why: It created easy drinking, ease of selection, and fun and adventure.

quiz.q: [yellow tail] grew mainly by stealing share from prestige wines.
quiz.why: It grew the market by attracting new wine drinkers.

quiz.q: A red ocean is characterized by:
options: Competitors fighting over a shrinking profit pool
quiz.why: Low margins, high stress, commodity survival.

quiz.q: The 'manager who lost the Coke account' example teaches:
options: Unconventional thinking can create a unique personal brand
quiz.why: Owning the failure could become a bold, unique selling proposition.

quiz.q: A value curve shows performance across an industry's accepted factors of competition.
quiz.why: Blue ocean strategy redraws it by questioning those factors.

case.title: The language school
case.scenario: A language school competes with dozens of others on the same factors: number of languages offered, certified teachers, textbook quality, classroom location, exam-prep certificates and price. Its adult students mostly want to have real conversations on trips and at work, and many quit after two months because classes feel like school.

questions.q: Apply the Four Actions Framework to design a blue ocean offer.
questions.model: Eliminate: textbooks and grammar-drill homework; maybe the downtown classroom. Reduce: number of languages (focus on the three most-requested), formal certification emphasis. Raise: speaking time per student, schedule flexibility. Create: real-world 'missions' (order at a partner restaurant, a mock job interview), conversation clubs with native speakers, a 'trip-ready in 8 weeks' guarantee.

questions.q: Who is the new customer this attracts, and why is it uncontested?
questions.model: Adults who don't think of themselves as 'students' and were never served by schools: travelers and professionals who hate classrooms. It's uncontested because rivals still compete on certifications and textbooks; the school now competes on outcomes like confidence and speaking that the others don't measure.

apply: Pick two competing products, a leader and an also-ran. What metrics do people judge them on, and what explains the gap?
Take a recent corporate PR disaster. What opportunity hides in it if you had to swim in those waters?
What tagline does your name currently evoke? What do you want it to evoke?

lectures.title: Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, Threats
lectures.hook: Act from knowledge, not impressions: PEST, five forces, value chain, then SWOT ties them together.

sections.h: Copperfield's Books and the great wheel
sections.html: Copperfield's Books (northern California, founded 1981) grew for 13 years, then stagnated in 1995. It sold the same products in the same places, but the environment had turned: megastores, Amazon, e-readers. Strategic thinking means replacing impressions with orderly reasoning about causes and effects. Four tools help.

• Political: government and regulation (zoning, tax, approval rules), and personally, the web of power relationships at work and home. The political tide shifts; swim with it.
  • Economic: are there enough customers willing to pay? Does the economy favor you or rivals?
  • Social: trends, fads, and deep long-term cultural factors; spot tomorrow's trends in today's indicators.
  • Technological: does technology support your plan or threaten it?

Usable, with tweaks, from computer industries to romantic relationships:

  • Buyer power: Copperfield's customers could buy identical books anywhere on price; little loyalty. High.
  • Supplier power: publishers gave chains volume discounts independents couldn't get. High for independents.
  • Rivalry: mature, low-growth industry with megastore consolidation. Intense.
  • Threat of substitutes: libraries, online, nonspecialist stores, TV, games. High.
  • Threat of new entrants: capital needs and low margins made it unattractive. Low.

Verdict: time to change the business model.

Break an organization into its value-producing activities to see what makes it strong or weak. A football team's win-loss record hides the contribution of each unit; disassemble offense, defense, coaching and personnel decisions against the mission. Do the same with your personal value chain. Firms and people outsource what they don't do well (Borders let Starbucks run its cafés; you don't sew your own clothes).

Value chain gives internal strengths and weaknesses; PEST and five forces give external opportunities and threats. SWOT combines them. For Copperfield's, a changing environment turned an old strength (thoughtful selection) into a weakness (lack of choice). Its answer: a uniquely local persona with book-buying and social experiences unavailable online or in megastores. Borders, an apparent winner, then failed to adapt: it outsourced online sales to Amazon, missed e-readers, and lost its Starbucks contract to Barnes & Noble. Same pressures, different responses.

takeaways: PEST scans the external macro environment.
Five forces: buyers, suppliers, rivalry, substitutes, new entrants.
Value chain reveals internal strengths and weaknesses; outsource non-core activities.
SWOT unites internal (S, W) and external (O, T).
Environment change can flip a strength into a weakness (Copperfield's selection).

terms.def: A scan of the political, economic, social and technological environment.
Porter's model: buyer power, supplier power, rivalry, threat of substitutes, threat of new entrants.
Breaking an organization (or person) into value-producing activities to find strengths and weaknesses.
Strengths and weaknesses (internal) combined with opportunities and threats (external).

quiz.q: Which tool looks inside the organization?
quiz.why: Value chain analysis evaluates internal activities; PEST and five forces look outward.

quiz.q: For Copperfield's Books, which force was LOW?
quiz.why: Capital requirements and low margins made entry unattractive.

quiz.q: In SWOT, opportunities and threats come from the external environment.
quiz.why: S and W are internal; O and T are external.

quiz.q: What did Copperfield's do to survive?
options: Built a local persona with experiences unavailable online
quiz.why: A uniquely local, social book-buying experience.

quiz.q: Which was one of Borders' mistakes?
options: Outsourcing its online sales to Amazon
quiz.why: It also missed e-readers and lost its Starbucks deal to Barnes & Noble.

quiz.q: A changing environment can turn a former strength into a weakness.
quiz.why: Copperfield's thoughtful selection became 'relative lack of choice.'

case.title: Career SWOT for a new graduate
case.scenario: Jonas just finished a business degree in Switzerland. He speaks German, English and Spanish, built a small e-commerce side business, but has weak Excel/data skills and no corporate internship. AI tools are automating junior analyst tasks, Swiss firms are expanding into Latin America, and hiring for generic junior roles is slow.

questions.q: Build Jonas's SWOT.
questions.model: Strengths: trilingual (incl. Spanish), real e-commerce experience, entrepreneurial initiative. Weaknesses: weak Excel/data skills, no corporate internship. Opportunities: Swiss firms expanding into Latin America; demand for people who can work with AI tools. Threats: AI automating junior analyst tasks; slow hiring for generic roles.

questions.q: What strategy does the SWOT suggest? Connect specific S/O and W/T pairs.
questions.model: S+O: market himself to Swiss firms entering Latin America as the bridge (language plus hands-on commerce), a differentiated rather than generic junior. W+T: close the data gap fast and learn to use AI tools to do analyst work faster, so automation becomes leverage rather than a replacement. Avoid the generic-junior red ocean.

apply: Scan your own environment (PEST), then inventory your personal value chain honestly. What actions follow?
Use PEST to explain what drove Apple and Amazon into competition over e-readers and tablets.
Apply value-chain thinking to a team or company you follow. What strategy does it suggest?

lectures.title: Avoid the Pathologies of Execution
lectures.hook: Five ways good plans die: no one responsible, overreach, broken communication, bad intelligence, inertia.

sections.html: September 1944: Montgomery's plan to seize six bridges behind German lines up to Arnhem and end the war. Its built-in flaw: everything had to go right. The Allies believed German resistance had broken; two panzer divisions were resting and refitting nearby, one at Arnhem itself. After nine days, withdrawal. The planners underestimated the enemy, overestimated themselves, and built a plan too tightly wound, with too many objectives, moving parts and coordination needs, plus wishful thinking that hid red flags.

1. Omission of responsibility: nothing happens when no one is responsible. Planners don't connect plans to specific tasks; the classic planning-execution gap.
  2. Overreach: capabilities and strategy don't align (Market Garden; Germany's Battle of the Bulge plan, which also needed everything to go right and underestimated the enemy's ability to interfere).
  3. Communication and coordination breakdown: the Charge of the Light Brigade (Balaklava, 1854). A vague order to "advance rapidly to the front... to prevent the enemy carrying away the guns" didn't say which guns; the cavalry charged straight at massed Russian artillery.
  4. Poor intelligence: the Dieppe raid (1942). Unclear objective ("learn lessons"), resurrected by Mountbatten without authorization, months-old intelligence, beach assessed from holiday snapshots, hidden German guns unknown, insufficient naval support and no bombing for political reasons. Only 15 tanks got off the beach; the Germans had been expecting a landing for weeks.
  5. Inertia: a body in motion stays on course, especially when egos and careers are invested. At the Somme (1916), a seven-day barrage warned the Germans and failed to destroy their defenses, yet Rawlinson let the attack proceed: 60,000 British casualties on the first day.

Jack Welch spent a full week every year, for 20 years, reviewing each GE unit's operating plan. You can't publish strategy and wait. Assign responsibility, avoid overreach, communicate clearly, nurture intelligence, and reject inertia when new information arrives. Strategy is a process, not an event. A decision has no effect unless action commitments are built in from the start; grand strategy must be translated into unit-level steps, with follow-through, checks and some "management by walking around."

takeaways: Plans that need everything to go right will fail.
Five pathologies: no responsibility, overreach, communication breakdown, poor intelligence, inertia.
Vague orders kill (Light Brigade); stale intelligence kills (Dieppe); sunk-cost momentum kills (Somme).
Build action commitments and named owners into every decision.
Control mechanisms (Welch's reviews) keep strategy alive.

terms.def: When strategy demands more than your capabilities can deliver, often from underestimating the opponent.
No one is assigned to execute, so nothing happens; the gap between planning and execution.
The tendency to stay on a set course, especially when egos are invested, even as it fails.
A specific, owned task built into a decision so that it actually takes effect.
1944 Allied plan to seize six bridges to Arnhem; failed through overreach and poor intelligence.

quiz.q: The Charge of the Light Brigade is the course's example of:
quiz.why: A vague order didn't specify which guns, so the cavalry charged the wrong way.

quiz.q: British planners assessed the Dieppe beach using:
quiz.why: Months-old, unreliable intelligence, including tourist photos.

quiz.q: At the Somme, Rawlinson canceled the attack when the barrage failed to destroy German defenses.
quiz.why: He let inertia take over and ordered the attack to proceed: 60,000 casualties.

quiz.q: Market Garden's 'built-in disadvantage' was that:
options: It required everything to go right
quiz.why: Tightly wound plans with many moving parts break at the first surprise.

quiz.q: Jack Welch's annual week of plan reviews illustrates:
quiz.why: A control mechanism to steer strategy to completion.

quiz.q: Per the lecture, a decision won't take effect unless action commitments are built in from the start.
quiz.why: If a decision is no one's specific work and responsibility, nothing happens.

case.title: The app relaunch
case.scenario: A team of five plans to relaunch their app in six weeks: new design, new payment system, a partnership with a bank that hasn't signed yet, launches in three countries, and a marketing campaign. The CEO's kickoff email says "Let's all make this happen!" with no owners named. Two weeks in, user tests show people hate the new design, but the CEO says it's too late to change direction.

questions.q: Which pathologies are present? Name at least four with evidence.
questions.model: Omission of responsibility: no owners, just 'let's all make this happen.' Overreach: five people, six weeks, five major workstreams; it needs everything to go right (the bank hasn't signed). Poor intelligence: assumes the bank deal and three markets without validation. Inertia: ignoring negative user tests because 'it's too late.' Likely communication breakdown too, with vague goals and no coordination plan.

questions.q: What control mechanism and changes would you put in place?
questions.model: Cut scope to what five people can do (one country, design fix, payments only if the bank signs: a branch plan). Name an owner and deadline for each workstream. Weekly 30-minute review against simple metrics, with pre-agreed triggers ("if user test scores are below X, we revise the design") so new information changes course instead of being rationalized away.

apply: Recall a time you were too optimistic about results. Was the plan too tightly wound, with no margin for error?
Find personal examples of each of the five pathologies. Would recognizing them have changed the outcome?
What control mechanism do you use to catch these pathologies early?

lectures.title: Tactics of Combat as Problem-Solving Tools
lectures.hook: Frontal assault, indirect approach, flank attack, rear area battle: pick the maneuver that fits the situation.

sections.html:
Strategy is the overall plan; tactics execute it. But you can't know in advance which details will become strategic. Intended strategy merges into emergent strategy through execution and responses to competitors. Richard Rumelt: "One person's strategy is another's tactics"; it depends where you sit. Execution is the neglected child of strategy. Ridgley calls the techniques strategic maneuvers.

Maneuvers apply from armies to individuals and from war to business and sports. In fencing they happen faster than conscious thought: you must abandon your line of attack when a better opening appears. Not every maneuver fits every situation.

An all-out attack on the enemy's front, usually on ground they chose and fortified. If it's your only option, mitigate: on D-Day the Allies had no alternative to the French coast, but deception hid the exact time and place. In business the frontal assault is the price war, and often only customers win. Attacking a strong, prepared enemy head-on violates almost every principle in the course.

Liddell Hart noted seven of eight frontal assaults in the Civil War failed. Keep opponents guessing between two equally attractive objectives, forcing them to split their forces to defend everything. Sherman's 1864 Georgia campaign kept Johnston unable to fix his objectives. Business: Honda mastered small engines first, then expanded horizontally into cars and caught Detroit napping.

Move to the enemy's side to dislocate them and force a disruptive response: Napoleon's specialty, MacArthur at Inch'ŏn, Sherman repeatedly forcing Johnston out of prepared positions. Lee's greatest victory, Chancellorsville (1863), paired a demonstration on the Union front with Jackson's march to the unsuspecting right flank.

In business, flanking often means a niche in a leader's blind spot. Royal Crown Cola failed in a frontal assault on Coke and Pepsi but flanked them with Diet Rite (1962), the best-selling soft drink by decade's end. It then failed to concentrate on its winner, tried to compete on both fronts, and Diet Rite faded when Diet Coke arrived.

Sow confusion behind the lines so no ground feels safe, forcing the opponent to spend resources defending what it thought was won. Commandos, the French Underground and Soviet partisans tied down German troops; German commandos in U.S. uniforms caused confusion at the Bulge. The psychological effect matters as much as the physical. Politics: campaigns strike rivals' home bases. History: the 1864 raid on Washington to relieve Cold Harbor. Business: Fujifilm attacked Kodak in the U.S. in the 1980s; Kodak counterattacked in Japan.

It depends on your position, resources, capabilities, risk tolerance and strategic intent. Knit engagements into a coherent whole; tactics without strategy is aimless conflict. Even a battle you'd win isn't worth fighting if it doesn't advance your strategy.

takeaways: Rumelt: strategy vs. tactics depends on where you sit; execution is strategy's neglected child.
Frontal assault = price war; avoid it, or mitigate with deception.
Indirect approach: threaten two objectives to split the defense (Sherman, Honda).
Flank: attack the niche or blind spot, then concentrate on the winner (RC Cola didn't).
Rear area battle: make the opponent defend its home base (Fuji vs. Kodak).

terms.def: The strategy that actually takes shape through execution and responses to events, as opposed to the intended plan.
An all-out attack on an opponent's prepared front; in business, the price war.
Moving against an opponent's side or blind spot to force a disruptive response.
Attacking an opponent's 'safe' ground behind the lines to force it to divert resources.
Strategy scholar: 'One person's strategy is another's tactics'; firms succeed by inventing or exploiting change.
British strategist of the indirect approach; championed the tank after WWI.
