quiz.why: Often the only winners are consumers.

quiz.q: Royal Crown's Diet Rite was a successful:
quiz.why: It flanked Coke and Pepsi with the first national diet soda.

quiz.q: RC Cola concentrated its resources on Diet Rite once it led the market.
quiz.why: It competed on both fronts, let the market choose, and Diet Rite faded after Diet Coke.

quiz.q: Fujifilm attacking Kodak in the U.S. is an example of:
quiz.why: Hitting the rival's home base; Kodak responded in Japan.

quiz.q: Keeping two equally attractive objectives in play aims to:
options: Force the opponent to split its forces
quiz.why: A technique of the indirect approach (Sherman in Georgia).

quiz.q: Rumelt argues that whether something is strategy or tactics depends on where you sit.
quiz.why: Corporate tactics can be a business unit's strategy.

case.title: Taking on the incumbent meal-kit brand
case.scenario: A young meal-kit company with limited funds faces a dominant competitor that owns the 'busy families' segment, spends heavily on discounts, and is strongest in big cities. The incumbent ignores vegetarians, small towns, and people with specific medical diets. Investors are pushing the startup to go head-to-head with a bigger discount.

questions.q: Evaluate the investors' suggestion using the lecture.
questions.model: It's a frontal assault on ground the incumbent chose and fortified, in the form of a price war against a rival with deeper pockets. It violates mass, economy of force and maneuver, and the likely winners are customers, not the startup.

questions.q: Propose a flank or indirect approach, and say what the startup must do once it works.
questions.model: Flank: own a blind spot, e.g. kits for medical diets (diabetic, low-FODMAP) or small-town delivery. Indirect: threaten two attractive niches so the incumbent can't defend both. Once one niche clearly wins, concentrate resources there (the RC Cola lesson) and fortify it before the incumbent copies it, rather than spreading across fronts.

apply: Do you always respond to problems the same way? Pick one maneuver you've never used and try it at the next opportunity.
What options did Lee have on the third day of Gettysburg besides Pickett's frontal charge?
Where could you create a new threat in an area your opponent thinks is secure?

lectures.title: Shock of the New—Inflection Points
lectures.hook: Some changes are hiccups; some change the rules of the game. Senior leaders usually spot the second kind last.

sections.h: What a strategic inflection point is
sections.html: Andy Grove (Intel) coined the term in Only the Paranoid Survive (1996): a dramatic change in your environment that forces you to change how you operate or risk extinction. The advantage goes to whoever recognizes and responds first, which connects back to PEST and five forces scanning. But advantage is temporary: the response diffuses, becomes best practice, and one firm's edge becomes everyone's parity.

Causes: technology, shifts in competition, customer preferences, regulation, raw-material prices. Grove warns senior management usually recognizes them last.

  • Talkies: within a decade of sound films, silent film production had stopped.
  • Airline deregulation (1978): freedom on fares, routes and entry was a bounty for consumers, but legacy airlines kept doing business as usual.
  • Kodak and Polaroid: digital imaging ended chemical film fast. Polaroid went bankrupt in 2001; Kodak sought bankruptcy protection in 2012.

The counterexample: Richard Harrington became CEO of Thomson Corporation in 1997, a profitable publishing grab bag with nearly $9 billion revenue. Seeing electronic publishing coming, he accepted a short-term earnings hit, spent $7 billion on 200+ businesses, shed 130+ regional newspapers, and within five years was challenging Elsevier in professional publishing.

Rule changes are inflection points, sometimes built from small steps: the chess queen was weak until rule changes in the 15th to 16th centuries made her the strongest piece, forcing new strategy. Football rule tweaks changed which players get recruited.

In politics: the two-term presidential limit created lame ducks; nomination power moved from conventions to primaries; new media (FDR on radio, Kennedy and Reagan on TV, Obama on the internet in 2008) reshaped campaigns. Even non-tech sectors face technology inflection points.

sections.h: In war: the Crusades and the Mongols
sections.html: The First Crusade (1095) hit Arab and Turkish armies with armor, heavy horses, siege machines and the crossbow, a technological and tactical surprise. In 1241 the Europeans were on the receiving end: Batu Khan's Mongols, with speed, unique supply, spies and scouts, and leaders protected at a distance, crushed the Hungarians. Only the death of the Great Khan Ögödei broke the invasion's tempo: fortune, not European adaptation, saved Europe.

The hard part is telling an inflection point from a historical hiccup, especially since we resist change. Grove's warning signs:

  • The key firm or player you deal with seems to have "shifted."
  • Your attention moves away from a lifelong competitor toward someone or something new.
  • The silver bullet test: if you had one bullet, where would you aim? If the answer has changed, it's more than a minor shift.

takeaways: A strategic inflection point changes the rules; respond or risk extinction.
First responders gain advantage, but it erodes into parity.
Leaders often see it last (Kodak, legacy airlines); bold reinvention works (Thomson).
Rule changes are inflection points too (the chess queen, primaries).
Grove's tests: things have 'shifted'; a new competitor worries you; your silver bullet changes target.

terms.def: Grove: a dramatic change in the environment that forces a change in strategy or risks extinction.
Grove's question: if you had one bullet, which competitor would you aim at? A changed answer signals an inflection point.
When an advantage has diffused and become standard practice, so no one gains from it.
Intel leader; author of Only the Paranoid Survive (1996), which named strategic inflection points.
Thomson CEO (from 1997) who transformed it into an electronic professional publisher.
Founder of the Mongol Empire who revolutionized 13th-century warfare.

quiz.q: Who coined 'strategic inflection point'?
quiz.why: In Only the Paranoid Survive (1996).

quiz.q: According to Grove, senior management usually recognizes inflection points first.
quiz.why: They usually recognize them last.

quiz.q: What did Thomson's Harrington do?
options: Took a short-term hit to move into electronic publishing
quiz.why: $7 billion in acquisitions and 130+ newspapers shed.

quiz.q: The chess queen example shows that inflection points can:
options: Build up from a series of small rule changes
quiz.why: Gradual rule changes made her the most powerful piece.

quiz.q: What stopped the Mongols from pushing deeper into Europe in 1241?
options: The death of the Great Khan Ögödei
quiz.why: Fortune, not adaptation, broke the invasion's tempo.

quiz.q: Competitive advantage from responding to an inflection point tends to be temporary.
quiz.why: It diffuses and becomes best practice, then parity.

case.title: The translation agency and AI
case.scenario: A 30-person translation agency had record revenue last year. This year, three long-time clients started running first drafts through AI and only buying 'review' services at half the price. A new competitor offering AI-plus-human editing at 40% lower prices keeps coming up in sales calls. The founder says it's a blip and that quality always wins.

questions.q: Apply Grove's warning signs. Is this an inflection point?
questions.model: Yes, very likely. Clients have 'shifted' (buying review instead of translation). Attention has moved to a new competitor that wasn't on the radar. Silver bullet: a year ago they'd aim at the other big agency; now they'd aim at the AI-hybrid firm. All three signals fire, and the founder's 'blip' framing is the classic senior-management-sees-it-last pattern, made worse by record revenue last year.

questions.q: What would a Harrington-style response look like?
questions.model: Accept a short-term earnings hit to rebuild the model: invest in an AI-plus-expert workflow, retrain translators as editors and domain specialists, reprice around speed and accuracy guarantees, and drop low-value general work while doubling down on high-stakes domains (legal, medical) where human review is required. Act before parity sets in.

apply: How could a company overcome blindness to inflection points when times are good?
Treat an inflection point as a rule change. What written and unwritten rules govern your competitive interactions, and could a new behavior within them give you an edge?
What do the rules of your game allow that nobody is doing yet?

lectures.title: Surprise! Perils and Power of Strategic Deception
lectures.hook: Surprise multiplies force; deception multiplies surprise. Five kinds: intention, time, place, strength, style.

sections.html: From the Trojan Horse to Pearl Harbor, Inch'ŏn and Schwarzkopf's "left hook" (1991), surprise is the goal and the stratagem (a trick to deceive the enemy) is the means. No other principle multiplies combat power as well. Great commanders from Hannibal to Stonewall Jackson used it. Between 1900 and WWII it fell out of favor, except for unconventional leaders like T. E. Lawrence (Arab Revolt, 1916 to 1918) and Churchill, a lover of deception and new technology.

Strategic surprise disrupts an enemy's mobilization, deployment and grand strategy; it is far harder because of scale, variables, time and chance of discovery. A failed strategic surprise can still be a tactical one, with much less impact.

The tank in 1916: Lt. Col. Ernest Swinton wanted tanks kept secret and used en masse to break through and hit enemy artillery. Generals ignored him and fed 32 tanks piecemeal across a broad front at the Somme: a little local panic, a minor tactical success, and a game-changing secret wasted. You only get one first use of a powerful new weapon.

Surprise is the gap between what we expect and what happens, deliberately created and exploited. Enemies don't just add uncertainty; deception gives you false certainty, false expectations or diverted attention. At Troy, the hollow horse was only half the trick: burning their camp and appearing to leave created the false expectation that made the horse work.

Tactical surprise pays out of all proportion to effort; strategic surprise is rarer but can deliver short- and long-term wins. Stealth and ambiguity help, but deception is the amplifier.

1. Intention: will they strike at all? The yes/no gateway to all others.
  2. Time: Pearl Harbor, while Japan's ambassador sought talks with Cordell Hull; Philip IV's arrest of the Knights Templar (1307); the Night of the Long Knives (1934); the political "October surprise."
  3. Place: Operation Bodyguard convinced Germany D-Day would hit the Pas-de-Calais; in 1991 a threatened Marine landing pinned Iraqi forces while the left hook swept through the desert.
  4. Strength: the Mongols showed only part of their force to lure attacks, appeared from flanks and rear, or faked size with extra campfires and dust clouds dragged by horses.
  5. Style: unexpected weapons or methods (the tank, Cannae, Delium). Surprise can be defensive too: Britain's undetected evacuation of Gallipoli.

Sports now treat scouting, film study and statistical analysis as part of the game, searching tendencies for weakness. Surprise is a double-edged sword: know the five types so you can see them coming.

takeaways: Surprise is a force multiplier; deception multiplies surprise.
Surprise = a deliberately created gap between expectation and reality.
Five types: intention, time, place, strength, style.
You get one first use of a new weapon; don't waste it piecemeal (tanks, 1916).
Defensive surprise exists (Gallipoli); know the types to defend against them.

terms.def: A trick designed to deceive the enemy in order to achieve surprise.
Surprise that disrupts an opponent's mobilization, deployment and overall strategy; rare and hard.
A factor that makes your existing capabilities far more effective, like surprise.
Allied deception before D-Day that made Germany expect the invasion at the Pas-de-Calais.
'Lawrence of Arabia'; led the Arab Revolt; wrote Seven Pillars of Wisdom on guerrilla tactics.
British officer who championed secret, massed use of the tank; ignored in 1916.

quiz.q: Which surprise type is the 'gateway' to all others?
quiz.why: Whether the enemy intends to strike at all.

quiz.q: The Mongols lighting extra campfires is an example of surprise of:
quiz.why: They masked or exaggerated their numbers.

quiz.q: In 1916 the British used tanks en masse, exactly as Swinton advised.
quiz.why: Only 32 were fed piecemeal across a broad front, wasting the strategic surprise.

quiz.q: Operation Bodyguard targeted which kind of surprise?
quiz.why: It shaped German expectations about where the invasion would land.

quiz.q: The lecture defines surprise as:
options: The gap between what we expect and what actually happens
quiz.why: And strategic surprise is a gap deliberately created and exploited.

quiz.q: The British evacuation of Gallipoli is an example of defensive surprise.
quiz.why: Surprise isn't only for offensive operations.

case.title: The product announcement
case.scenario: A startup has built a feature its much larger competitor doesn't have and can't copy for about six months. The team wants to announce it right away in a blog post and on social media 'to build hype,' then release it gradually over three months to small groups of users.

questions.q: What lesson from the 1916 tank story applies here?
questions.model: You only get one first use of a game changer. Announcing early and releasing piecemeal is the 1916 tank mistake: it tells the competitor what's coming, starts their six-month clock early, and spreads the impact thin, so you get local buzz instead of a breakthrough.

questions.q: Design a launch that uses at least three of the five types of surprise.
questions.model: Intention: keep the project quiet so the competitor doesn't think you're entering this space. Time: launch right before the competitor's busy season or big conference. Place: launch first in the segment where the competitor is weakest. Strength: release fully to all target users at once with sales and support ready (mass). Style: package it in a way the market doesn't expect, e.g. free for switchers.

apply: What information do you control exclusively, and would results change if you handled its timing differently?
How might the timing of an announcement, against an opponent's expectations, strengthen your position?
Where have you become so predictable that opponents can counter you easily? Break the routine once on purpose.

lectures.title: The Sources and Uses of Reliable Intelligence
lectures.hook: Intelligence is analyzed information you actually act on. Run the cycle and resist the Cassandra curse.

sections.html: In Star Wars (1977) an intelligence officer analyzes the rebel attack and advises evacuation; the commander refuses because victory seems near. We want certainty, yet we reject reliable information that conflicts with our biases. Leonard Fuld: actively seek intelligence and learn to use it, and information becomes a weapon.

Intelligence is analyzed information, not raw information. Spying (human intelligence, "humint") is only one part of intelligence, which is only one part of strategy. NFL teams spend millions on scouting, tendency charts and scenario questions (legal if from open sources; stealing signals is not). Political parties run "opposition research" on tax liens, lawsuits and voting records, timed for maximum effect.

Former CIA analyst Jan Herring's five uses of intelligence analysis: (1) early warning to prevent surprise, (2) supporting decisions, (3) competitor assessment and monitoring, (4) planning and strategy development, (5) supporting collection and reporting.

It targets three elements of friends, enemies and yourself: resources, capabilities, intentions. In football: resources = money, draft picks, contacts; capabilities = developed resources visible as strengths and weaknesses; intentions = how they'll use them against you.

1. Planning and priority intelligence requirements: decide what to collect and what to ignore, so research doesn't become endless procrastination.
  2. Collection: systematic and multi-source (databases, trade shows, press releases, ex-employees, overheard conversations). Don't rely only on comfortable sources.
  3. Analysis: part art; use multiple tools (PEST, five forces, value chain, SWOT, competitor, political risk and scenario analysis). Never rely on one.
  4. Dissemination: where many efforts fail by delivering facts without analysis or relevance. Beware "nice-to-know" syndrome; intelligence is perishable.
  5. Action: needs courage: "This means we should..."

The cycle is virtuous: each turn sharpens the next. Its speed depends on how critical and time-pressed the issue is.

Apollo gave Cassandra prophecy, then cursed her never to be believed. The paradox of leadership: the qualities that make strong senior leaders (confidence, conviction) also make them reject informed advice.

A Union private found a copy of Lee's orders showing his army was split. McClellan saw the chance to destroy Lee and perhaps end the war, but moved too slowly, probably overestimating Lee's strength. Result: indecisive Antietam, the bloodiest day in U.S. military history, and two and a half more years of war. Lesson: when high-quality intelligence arrives, act boldly, correctly and quickly.

takeaways: Intelligence = analyzed, actionable information; spying is a small part.
Assess resources, capabilities and intentions (yours too).
Cycle: requirements, collection, analysis, dissemination, action.
Failure points: 'nice-to-know' dissemination and lack of courage to act.
Cassandra curse / McClellan: great intelligence is wasted without boldness.

terms.def: Information that has been analyzed for relevance to a decision, as opposed to raw facts.
Planning/requirements, collection, analysis, dissemination, action; repeated to sharpen focus.
The defined questions that decide what information to collect and what to ignore.
Delivering collected facts without analysis or relevance to action.
Having accurate foresight that no one believes; leaders rejecting intelligence that contradicts their views.
The three things intelligence aims to learn about competitors, allies and yourself.
Former CIA analyst who identified five uses of intelligence analysis.

quiz.q: What's the correct order of the intelligence cycle?
quiz.why: Five steps ending in action.

quiz.q: Intelligence and information are the same thing.
quiz.why: Intelligence is analyzed information.

quiz.q: 'Nice-to-know syndrome' is a failure at which stage?
quiz.why: Facts are presented with minimal analysis and relevance.

quiz.q: McClellan at Antietam shows that:
options: Great intelligence needs bold, fast action
quiz.why: He moved too slowly and squandered a pivotal advantage.

quiz.q: The paradox of leadership is that:
options: The traits of strong leaders make them reject informed advice
quiz.why: Confidence and conviction cut both ways.

quiz.q: Setting priority intelligence requirements helps prevent research from becoming procrastination.
quiz.why: It gives direction so you don't collect aimlessly.

case.title: The competitor's hiring spree
case.scenario: You lead product at a project-management software company. Over two months you notice: your main competitor posted 12 job ads for 'healthcare compliance' engineers, its CEO spoke at a hospital-IT conference, and two of your sales reps lost deals to it at clinics. Your CEO says they're a general tool like us and that healthcare is a distraction for them.

questions.q: Run this through the intelligence cycle. What are your priority requirements, and what do the clues suggest?
questions.model: Requirements: Is the competitor entering healthcare as a focus? When? With what product? Collection: job ads, conference talk, lost-deal notes, plus ex-employees, press releases, partner announcements. Analysis: resources (hiring budget), capabilities (compliance engineering), and intentions (CEO's healthcare positioning) all point the same way: a focused move into healthcare, possibly flanking you. Dissemination: a one-page brief with the implication, not a pile of facts. Action: decide whether to defend, partner or concede that segment.

questions.q: How do you avoid the Cassandra curse with your CEO?
questions.model: Bring analysis tied to a decision and money (lost clinic deals, pipeline at risk), not 'nice-to-know' facts. Present it as testable: name the indicators that would confirm or refute it within 60 days. Propose a small, low-cost action so the CEO can act without fully abandoning their view.

apply: What's an example from your life where analysis, not just information, explained a situation?
Using resources/capabilities/intentions, assess your toughest competitor. Do stated aims match their resources?
Build your own intelligence cycle with three priority requirements and run it monthly.

lectures.title: Move and Countermove—The Theory of Games
lectures.hook: Your best move depends on their move. Game theory structures that, as long as you remember people aren't always 'rational.'

sections.html: Thomas Schelling's game: two strangers win $1,000 each if they meet in New York City, with no communication and 30 seconds to answer. Most pick Times Square, Grand Central or the Empire State Building, at noon. With more time and information, answers scatter: more information can reduce clarity. With little information, we fall back on shared logic (focal points).

A game is a situation where several goal-oriented decision makers interact, and each one's outcome depends on the others' actions. Driving in traffic, asking for a raise and campaigning are games. Game theory began with John von Neumann analyzing bluffing in poker (1920s); with Morgenstern he later claimed it could ground economics. It builds mathematical models assuming rational actors who maximize utility (highest payoff or least damage): cost-benefit analysis applied to the mind.

sections.h: The Prisoner's Dilemma and the Cold War
sections.html: Two prisoners, questioned separately, choose to stay silent (cooperate) or implicate the other (defect). Both silent: light sentences. Both defect: longer sentences. One defects: the defector goes free and the cooperator gets the worst outcome. Defection is the dominant strategy because cooperation is too risky. Game theorists saw the nuclear arms race as this game: the advantage went to a successful first strike, making a tiny misstep catastrophic.

Opponents may seem irrational because they play for different stakes, or they may feign irrationality because it is rational to do so. In the $20 bill auction, the top two bidders both pay, so they keep bidding past $20 just to cut losses.

We also misjudge payoffs: colleagues may want money, recognition or authority. Mirror-imaging means assuming opponents share your values. McNamara played a rational limited war of carrots and sticks in Vietnam; the Vietnamese played a total war of national liberation.

Tragedy of the Commons (Garrett Hardin): each herder gets all the benefit of an extra cow while the damage is shared, so rational individuals overgraze the common pasture. National parks are a modern commons. Game theory calls the pattern CC-PP: commonize costs, privatize profits (e.g. a firm dumping waste in a river).

Free rider problem: the keg runs dry, the hat goes around, and the rational student knows the new keg arrives whether or not they chip in. It's a collective action problem; one fix is designing incentives that align individual and group goals.

Game theory makes you think about payoffs and stakes, and whether everyone sees them the same way. Its artificial assumption of rationality is a weakness in daily life. It also shows cooperative alternatives to pure conflict that can maximize outcomes for all sides.

takeaways: A game: interdependent goal-directed decisions; your payoff depends on others' moves.
Prisoner's Dilemma: defection dominates in a one-shot game.
Apparent irrationality may be rational for different stakes or feigned on purpose.
Avoid mirror-imaging: others may play a different game (Vietnam).
Commons, CC-PP and free riders: individual rationality can wreck group outcomes.

terms.def: A situation where several goal-oriented decision makers interact and outcomes depend on each other's choices.
Game theory's assumption that each player acts to maximize their own payoff (utility).
Two-player game where defecting is individually dominant though mutual cooperation pays better.
A choice that gives a better payoff no matter what the other player does.
Behavior that looks irrational but is rational given the player's stakes, or is feigned for effect.
Assuming an opponent shares your values and incentives.
Individuals rationally overuse a shared resource because benefits are private and costs shared.
People benefit from a shared good without contributing to it; a collective action problem.
Game theorist and strategist of the nuclear era; the 'meet in New York' focal-point game.
Mathematician who founded game theory by analyzing bluffing in poker.

quiz.q: In a one-shot Prisoner's Dilemma, the dominant strategy is:
quiz.why: Defecting pays more whatever the other does.

quiz.q: In Schelling's game, giving people more time and information made their answers converge more.
quiz.why: Answers scattered; more information reduced clarity.

quiz.q: Assuming your opponent shares your values is called:
quiz.why: McNamara in Vietnam is the course example.

quiz.q: CC-PP stands for:
quiz.why: Hardin's description of the commons dynamic in private enterprise.

quiz.q: Why do bidders in the $20 auction go above $20?
options: They are minimizing losses since second place also pays
They want to help the auctioneer

case.title: The shared office kitchen
case.scenario: Eight small startups share a coworking floor with a kitchen. Coffee and snacks are paid from a voluntary jar. The jar is always short, the kitchen is a mess, and the coworking manager threatens to remove the coffee machine. Each founder says they'd chip in more 'if others did.'

questions.q: Which game-theory problems does this illustrate, and why do rational people behave this way?
questions.model: A free rider problem (coffee appears whether or not you pay) and a Tragedy of the Commons (each person enjoys the benefit of using the kitchen while the mess is shared). Each founder rationally reasons their contribution makes little difference; individually rational choices produce a bad group outcome, likely losing the coffee entirely.

questions.q: Redesign the incentives so cooperation becomes the rational choice.
questions.model: Turn it into a club good: a small monthly fee per startup added to rent (no free riding), or a coffee machine that needs a team card. Make use visible (a cleaning rota per team, posted publicly) so reputations matter in a repeated game. Tie a clear consequence (losing kitchen access) to defection.

apply: Which ongoing game-like interactions do you have at work? What's really going on in them?
Can you put numbers on the payoffs in those games? Are you usually winning or losing?
How could you change the payoffs or the structure of a game to improve your position?

lectures.title: The Evolution of Cooperation
lectures.hook: In repeated games, cooperation can emerge between rivals, and even enemies. Tit for tat shows how.

sections.html: On the first Christmas of WWI, Germans placed lit Christmas trees on their trench parapets; greetings crossed no man's land; at dawn soldiers came out to bury the dead and then mingled freely. Despite both high commands, the truce lasted the day and in places several days. Research shows why: small units facing each other for long periods, which made communication and reciprocity possible.

Robert Axelrod's The Evolution of Cooperation (1984) asked what conditions let cooperation emerge among self-interested players. He studied trench warfare and the U.S. Senate, where rivals like Orrin Hatch and Ted Kennedy found ways to reciprocate and compromise.

Back to the Prisoner's Dilemma with payoffs: both defect $1 each, both cooperate $3 each, defector $5 and cooperator $0. Defection dominates in a single game. But when the same players meet repeatedly, a simple strategy wins: tit for tat. Cooperate first, then copy the other player's previous move.

sections.h: Five conditions for tit for tat
sections.html:
1. Avoid unnecessary conflict: cooperate as long as the other side does.
  2. Respond quickly to an uncalled-for defection.
  3. Forgive after responding.
  4. Be clear so the other player can recognize your pattern.
  5. Expect an indefinite number of interactions: the "shadow of the future."

Reciprocity wins by eliciting cooperation, not by beating the other player. It's especially useful abroad where detailed contracts are uncommon.

• The Washington-Moscow hotline (1963), after the Cuban missile crisis.
  • Late Cold War confidence- and security-building measures, including mutual inspection of exercises, because exercises can be misread as attacks or can mask real ones (the 1968 invasion of Czechoslovakia).
  • The Korean DMZ (150+ miles long, 2.5 wide): a cease-fire, not a peace, yet routinized cooperation at P'anmunjŏm.
  • KGB general Alexei Kondaurov signaled to dissidents which line would provoke police, and they respected it: live and let live.

Against the drift to disorder, spontaneous order says structure can emerge from self-interested people who aren't trying to build it: a dirt path across a meadow, or the price-regulated market economy.

Firms often avoid unilateral moves to escape painful responses; price wars show what happens when tacit cooperation breaks. A strategic alliance aligns firms' actions for synergy (whole greater than the sum of parts). When regulators blocked AT&T's 2011 purchase of T-Mobile, the two arranged spectrum access and coverage expansion instead.

takeaways: Repeated interaction (the shadow of the future) makes cooperation rational.
Tit for tat: cooperate first, then mirror the last move.
Conditions: be nice, retaliate fast, forgive, be clear, expect more rounds.
Even enemies cooperate when miscommunication costs more than cooperation (hotline, CSBMs).
Spontaneous order and alliances: structure and synergy can emerge without central design.

terms.def: Strategy for repeated games: cooperate first, then copy the other player's previous move.
The expectation of future interactions that makes cooperation worthwhile now.
Social order emerging from self-interested individuals who aren't trying to create it (a meadow path, markets).
Firms aligning their strategic actions because cooperation beats unfettered competition.
When a combined result is greater than the sum of its parts.
Political scientist; The Evolution of Cooperation (1984); showed tit for tat's success in repeated games.

quiz.why: Cooperate on the first move, then copy the other player's last move.

quiz.q: Using the lecture's payoffs, what do both players get if both cooperate?
quiz.why: $3 each; $1 each if both defect; $5 vs $0 if they split.

quiz.q: Tit for tat works best when players expect only one interaction.
quiz.why: It needs an indefinite number of interactions.

quiz.q: Why did the 1914 truce emerge, per research?
options: Small units faced each other for long periods
Both sides ran out of ammunition
quiz.why: Long-term proximity enabled communication and reciprocity.

quiz.q: Mutual inspections of military exercises were introduced because:
options: Exercises could be mistaken for, or used to mask, an invasion
quiz.why: The Soviets used an exercise as cover to invade Czechoslovakia in 1968.

quiz.q: A dirt path across a meadow is the lecture's example of spontaneous order.
quiz.why: No one designed it; many people's choices created it.

case.title: Two rival bakeries on one street
case.scenario: Two bakeries face each other on a busy street. Last month Bakery A cut croissant prices by 30%; Bakery B matched and went lower. Now both are losing money on croissants. Both owners plan to stay on this street for years. They also both complain about high flour prices from the same supplier.

questions.q: Explain the situation in Prisoner's Dilemma terms, and why it can be escaped.
questions.model: Each owner's dominant short-term move was to defect (undercut), producing mutual defection: both lose money. But it's a repeated game with a long shadow of the future (years on the same street), which makes tit for tat and reciprocal cooperation rational.

questions.q: Design a tit-for-tat approach and one cooperative move that creates synergy (without illegal price-fixing).
questions.model: Bakery A signals cooperation by quietly returning to a normal price and differentiating (sourdough focus) instead of undercutting; if B keeps undercutting, A responds quickly, then forgives once B stops; A keeps its behavior clear and predictable. Synergy: jointly buy flour from a cheaper supplier or as a buying group to cut costs for both, and co-promote the street (a weekend market), growing the pie instead of slicing it. Explicit price-fixing stays off the table.

apply: Think of your most intractable opponent. Design a tit-for-tat exercise and try it.
How can you lengthen the 'shadow of the future' with someone so their defection becomes less likely?
What made it possible for enemy soldiers to mingle freely in 1914 without orders?

lectures.title: When Strategy Breaks Down
lectures.hook: Smart organizations do dumb things: strategic masquerade, misalignment, groupthink, politics, overconfidence, loss of focus.

sections.html: Kodak dominated film via focused R&D and even patented the first digital camera in 1975, then chose not to develop it. It bought digital firms without changing its strategic focus; disposable cameras in the late 1980s reinforced the belief that film was the bedrock. It had nondigital core competencies and a slow-moving industry history. A possible path: lead the output side of digital, finished prints. Facing an inflection point, it stayed the course.

Good strategy closes options; Kodak was never going to dominate all of digital. A strategic masquerade substitutes slogans or operational techniques (TQM, benchmarking, best practices, Six Sigma) for real strategic choices. Strip those away and strategy is the ability to make tradeoffs: do some things and not others. Efficiency programs push the industry's efficiency frontier forward but don't create advantage. Personally, procrastination and routine busywork are masquerades: we feel strategic while absorbed in minor tasks, often from a desire to keep all options open.

• Internal: resources, capabilities and intentions don't mesh, or structure, operations and strategy don't. Personally: goals without the resources or capabilities, and without honesty about that gap.
  • External: the environment shifts slowly with no explosion. Generals "fight the last war": rifles and minié balls made frontal assault suicidal in the Civil War, and Europe repeated it in WWI.
  • Strategy creep (dilution, erosion): chasing every change without focus; people and resources get add-on tasks until stretched to breaking.

• Groupthink: excessive agreement; group values assumed right; no room to dissent.
  • Bureaucratic politics: insufficient agreement; leaders bargain for power and the output is a suboptimal compromise. DEC (1992): the CEO demanded consensus on focus, none came, and a non-strategy was announced.
  • Overconfidence: overestimating our judgment; assuming we understand new information without analysis.
  • Loss of focus: cause and symptom of erosion, often born from success, "building on our success," or hiring someone to "shake things up." Brand equity can't be extended, only diluted (Coca-Cola means soft drink).

A new marketing head arrived in April 2005 to "shake things up." By August, Walmart was buying Vogue ads at nearly $1 million per issue, then supercenters, remodeling, decluttering, organics, an upmarket push, and higher prices. The cause: overconfidence and mission creep, losing focus on "saving people money so they can live better." The cure for all these pathologies: steer a bold course and keep your eyes on the strategic goal.

takeaways: Kodak invented digital and still lost: staying the course at an inflection point.
Strategic masquerade: efficiency tools and slogans pretending to be strategy; real strategy = tradeoffs.
Misalignment: internal, external (fighting the last war), and strategy creep.
Conspirators: groupthink, bureaucratic politics, overconfidence, loss of focus.
Brand equity can't be extended, only diluted (Walmart in Vogue).

terms.def: Substituting slogans or operational techniques (TQM, benchmarking) for real strategic choices.
Deciding to do some things and not others; the heart of strategic management.
Gradual dilution of strategy as people and resources take on unfocused add-on tasks.
Excessive agreement in a group that suppresses dissent and lets bad ideas thrive.
Decisions as the outcome of bargaining among leaders rather than rational analysis.
Planning based on past conflicts while ignoring changes such as new technology.

case.title: The student who is 'very busy'
case.scenario: Lena wants to get into a top master's program in two years. Her week: color-coding her notes, reorganizing her study app, joining a fourth student club 'for networking,' taking every extra shift her part-time job offers, and reading productivity blogs. Her grades are flat, and she hasn't researched the programs' admission criteria.

questions.q: Diagnose Lena's situation with concepts from this lecture.
questions.model: Strategic masquerade: she substitutes technique (notes, apps, productivity reading) for strategy and feels busy instead of progressing. Strategy creep: club number four and every extra shift are add-ons that dilute focus. Internal misalignment: her intention (top program) isn't matched by resources or capabilities (grades, a test score, research). Poor intelligence: she doesn't know the admission criteria. She's keeping all options open instead of making tradeoffs.

questions.q: What tradeoffs should she make?
questions.model: First run the intelligence: list the 3 to 5 target programs and their real criteria. Then cut: quit two clubs, cap work shifts, stop tool-tinkering. Mass her time on what moves admission (GPA in key courses, test prep, one relevant project or internship, two strong recommenders). Saying no is the strategy.

apply: Do you absorb yourself in detailed execution instead of real strategic thinking? Where?
Which management tools in your workplace or school have substituted for an actual strategy?
What difficult tradeoffs have you made in your personal strategy? If none, reexamine your plan.

lectures.title: Leverage Cognitive Psychology for Better Strategy
lectures.hook: Your brain filters reality before you ever 'decide.' Know the filters, and break the mind rut on purpose.

sections.html: We think we're rational, but we rarely think about thinking. Perception, memory and how we blend it with new information all run without conscious direction; we see only the results. The classic model said we weigh options and maximize utility. Herbert Simon corrected it with bounded rationality: limits of information, cognition and time. The brain pre-filters input using experience, education and culture, builds a simplified mental model, and we act rationally only within that model, which can be badly off in high-stress, high-stakes moments.

sections.h: Mindsets and the expert's blind spot
sections.html: CIA veteran Richards Heuer: an experienced specialist may be among the last to see what's really happening when events turn; "analysts who know the most about a subject have the most to unlearn." In 1989 to 1990 CIA specialists were slow to grasp the speed of German reunification; generalists saw it. A mindset is a set of assumptions and methods; entrenched across a group, it becomes groupthink. Example: the Cold War mindset that led the U.S. to ally with unsavory regimes.

1. Mindsets form quickly but resist change. The "mind rut": a sequence of gradually distorted images hides that the last one is a different subject.
  2. We perceive what we expect to perceive. The Luftwaffe chief denied the Allies had a long-range fighter even after one was shot down; Stalin refused reports of the 1941 German invasion.
  3. New information is assimilated to existing images. Before the 1973 Arab-Israeli war, analysts updated each day's story incrementally, an "assembly line" narrative instead of the big picture.

Concern for solidarity and consensus degrades decisions (Bay of Pigs, the Watergate cover-up). Eight symptoms in three clusters (overestimating the group's power and morality; closed-mindedness; pressure to conform):

  • Illusion of invulnerability (excess optimism, risk taking)
  • Unquestioned belief in the group's morality
  • Rationalizing away warnings
  • Stereotyping opponents as weak, evil or stupid
  • Self-censorship of dissent
  • Illusion of unanimity
  • Direct pressure on dissenters, framed as "disloyalty"
  • Self-appointed "mind guards" shielding the group from dissenting information

Results: incomplete survey of alternatives, unexamined risks, rejected options never revisited, poor and biased information search, no contingency plans.

1. Define the problem so the answer makes a difference.
  2. Suspend judgment; list all plausible hypotheses, then trim to a workable set.
  3. Collect information on all of them, including alternatives you haven't seriously considered.
  4. Argue against the hypotheses: try to reject rather than confirm; evidence that fits your favorite may fit others too.
  5. Monitor for surprises: conclusions are tentative; name critical indicators to watch.

To generate hypotheses outside your mind rut, use: situational logic (inductive; treat this case as unique), application of theory (deductive; general to specific), comparison with historical situations (case studies), and data immersion (soak in data, suppress preconceptions, test emerging patterns).

takeaways: Bounded rationality: we decide inside a simplified mental model.
Experts have the most to unlearn (Heuer).
Barriers: sticky mindsets, seeing what we expect, assimilating new info to old images.
Janis's groupthink: eight symptoms around invulnerability, closed minds, conformity.
Analytical model: define, hypothesize widely, collect, try to reject, monitor.

terms.def: Simon's idea that decisions are rational only within limits of information, cognition and time.
A collection of assumptions and methods that shapes what a person or group sees.
Being locked into a pattern so that genuinely new information looks like a variation of the old.
Self-appointed group members who shield the group from dissenting information (a groupthink symptom).
Inductive analysis treating a situation as unique rather than as one of a class.
Soaking in data while suppressing preconceptions so patterns can emerge and be tested.
Social scientist who introduced bounded rationality.
CIA veteran; Psychology of Intelligence Analysis.
Psychologist who identified and named groupthink.

options: Analysts who know the most about the subject
quiz.why: Specialists were slower than generalists to see German reunification coming.

options: We perceive what we expect to perceive
quiz.why: His belief in the nonaggression paradigm overrode the evidence.

quiz.q: In the analytical process model you should try to confirm your favorite hypothesis.
quiz.why: Try to reject hypotheses rather than confirm them.

options: New information assimilated to existing images
quiz.why: Daily incremental updates prevented a coherent big picture.

quiz.q: Which is a symptom of groupthink?
quiz.why: Others: invulnerability, self-censorship, mind guards, pressure on dissenters.

quiz.why: Situational logic is the inductive counterpart.

case.title: The confident launch team
case.scenario: A marketing team of five has worked together for years and has never had a failed campaign. For a new market, they agree within ten minutes on the same campaign that worked at home. One junior member mentions that local focus groups found the humor offensive; the team lead says, "They just don't get it yet. We always win." Nobody raises it again, and there's no backup plan.

questions.q: Identify the groupthink symptoms and perception barriers at work.
questions.model: Illusion of invulnerability ('we always win'), rationalizing warnings (focus group dismissed), stereotyping the audience ('they don't get it'), self-censorship (nobody raises it again), illusion of unanimity (ten-minute agreement), direct pressure on the dissenter. Perception barriers: they see what they expect (home success), assimilating new market data to the old image. No contingency plan is a typical groupthink output.

questions.q: Apply the analytical process model to fix the decision.
questions.model: Define the problem: what campaign will work in THIS market? List several hypotheses (adapt the humor, a different tone, a local partner). Collect information for each, including the focus group. Try to reject the favored home campaign: does any evidence contradict it? Set indicators to monitor (early engagement, complaints) and a backup campaign. Assign someone as devil's advocate.

apply: Is there a consensus 'groupthink' on some public issue you follow? Where did it come from?
Do you feel pressure to conform in your team? Who decides the central ideas?
How do you define problems in group settings? Is the definition rigged toward the answer you want?
Which cognitive trap affects you most, and how will you guard against it?

lectures.title: Strategic Intuition and Creative Insight
lectures.hook: Coup d'oeil is not magic. It's pattern memory plus courage, and it can be trained.

sections.html: Clausewitz's "stroke of the eye" is the flash of insight behind great strategy, obvious in hindsight. Scientists no longer see analysis and intuition as separate; a single mode of thought, intelligent memory, combines them. Research suggests we can cultivate insight by creating the conditions that produce it.

The textbook model has four steps: analyze the problem, list options, weight criteria and evaluate, add up the score. William Duggan: decision makers use that only when procedures force them; left alone, they use strategic intuition. Military research separates analytical decisions (when there's time) from intuitive ones (when time is short), but intuition is weak with inexperienced leaders, very complex situations, or competing courses of action.

Gary Klein: experts don't generate many options and pick one. Problem and solution come to them together; they mentally simulate the course of action and commit or reject it.

Duggan's definition: strategic intuition is the "selective projection of past elements into the future in a new combination," with personal commitment to follow through and work out details along the way. That matches Porter's "doing things differently."

If everyone follows the same best practices, the efficiency frontier moves and nobody gains lasting advantage. The Civil War was close to a controlled experiment: officers from the same academy, same teachers, same prior war. The North had overwhelming material superiority, yet the war lasted four years. At Chancellorsville (May 1863), Lee faced Hooker's army twice his size, entrenched and better supplied, and won the most lopsided contest of the war by violating a bedrock rule: never divide your army in the face of a superior foe. Two divisions held Hooker while Jackson marched around the Union right.

Klein found experienced firefighters don't compare options; they act. Intuition is the gradual build-up of a large repertoire of patterns over years of practice. Without it, decision makers freeze. Formal analysis supplements intuition but can't replace it. Klein's balance: let intuition recognize and decide, and use analysis to verify.

sections.h: Seven steps to develop intuitive insight
sections.html:
1. Your first option is probably the best: note it, then mentally simulate how it would play out and what could go wrong.
  2. Make sure you understand the problem.
  3. Override intuition when it misleads: ask what evidence would change your mind. If nothing could, you've built a cocoon.
  4. Use intuition to think ahead of the curve: connect dots, flag inconsistencies.
  5. Accept uncertainty; know when you have enough to act.
  6. Use the right strategy: if it's complicated and nobody has good intuitions, analyze.
  7. Watch out for naysayers: managers who discount experience, demand blind compliance, can't tolerate uncertainty.

Insight isn't reserved for Napoleon or Steve Jobs; recombining what you know in new ways is a learnable skill.

takeaways: Analysis and intuition merge in 'intelligent memory.'
Experts recognize problem and solution together (Klein), then mentally simulate.
Strategic intuition = new combinations of past elements projected forward (Duggan).
Lee at Chancellorsville: insight beat textbook rules and superior resources.
Intuition decides, analysis verifies; build patterns through deliberate experience.

Duggan: selectively projecting past elements into the future in a new combination, with commitment to follow through.
Klein's finding that experts recognize a situation and a workable action together, then mentally test it.
Columbia strategist; Strategic Intuition and Napoleon's Glance.
Research psychologist who studied firefighters' intuition; The Power of Intuition.

options: Leaders are inexperienced or the situation is very complex
The expert has seen similar cases
quiz.why: Also when there are competing courses of action.

options: Intuition recognizes and decides, analysis verifies
quiz.why: Combine them, with intuition first.

quiz.why: Step 3: override intuition when it misleads.

case.title: The overanalyzed hire
case.scenario: A team lead with 12 years of hiring experience meets a candidate and immediately feels 'this person is right,' though the candidate's CV is unusual. HR insists on a 20-criteria weighted scorecard; the candidate scores slightly below another applicant. The lead is also known for occasionally falling for charismatic interviewees.

questions.q: When should the lead trust this intuition, according to Klein and the seven steps?
questions.model: The lead has a big repertoire of patterns from 12 years, so the first impression deserves to be recorded and taken seriously (step 1). But they should mentally simulate the hire (first 90 days, where it could fail) and ask what evidence would change their mind (step 3), especially given the known charisma bias. Intuition recognizes; analysis verifies.

questions.q: Propose a process that combines intuition and analysis instead of choosing one.
questions.model: Let intuition name the hypothesis ('this candidate will outperform'), then verify with targeted analysis: a work-sample task, reference calls aimed at the charisma risk, and a check of the two or three criteria that really predict success rather than all 20. If verification holds, hire despite the scorecard; if it exposes the known bias, override the gut.

apply: Do you dismiss intuition as unworthy? How could you listen more to your voice of experience?
Where do you simply 'know' the answer within your expertise? How could coup d'oeil help you act on it?
Compare the strengths and limits of analytical and intuitive decision-making in one decision you face now.

lectures.title: From Systemic Problems to Systemic Solutions
lectures.hook: If it's the same problem as last year, it's a system problem. Fix the system, not the symptom.

sections.html: Drucker called them "recurring crises." John Foster Dulles: "The measure of success is not whether you have a tough problem to deal with, but whether it is the same problem you had last year." A system is a collection of people, processes and things that interact as an integrated whole, with structure, behavior, interdependence and usually output. Garbage collection, power grids, legal systems: we use them without seeing them, holding only expectations. It pays to look.

John A. Warden III argued all systems share five components, drawn as concentric circles from the center out:

  1. Leader
  2. Conversion process (food or energy that keeps it running)
  3. Infrastructure (blood vessels, roads, transmission lines)
  4. Population
  5. Action units (antibodies, police, maintenance crews)

It works for a body, a state or a drug cartel, and lets you ask: what is the system's purpose, and does it deliver it?

In 1999 Lou Gerstner saw IBM winning more U.S. patents than anyone (1993 to 1999) but not turning them into businesses. His task force found that the short-term profit focus created strategic myopia; managers weren't rewarded for spotting growth; demands for fact-based analysis and detailed forecasts created a climate of fear; new ventures were held to legacy-business earnings targets and had their budgets cut. The system was designed to deliver stability, not new businesses. The Emerging Business Opportunities program changed incentives; 22 successful businesses launched in its first five years.

Jeff Severts saw that sales forecasts were tangled with budgeting, performance measurement, compensation and purchasing, each with an agenda that skewed the numbers. Borrowing James Surowiecki's wisdom-of-crowds idea, he asked 190 employees for estimates: off by less than 0.5%; a later test was 99.9% accurate. The system's incentives, not bad luck, had produced bad forecasts.

In the village of Sujala, the Byrraju Foundation fought disease not with more doctors or medicine but by installing water purification, and disease plummeted. Hindustan Unilever paired cheaper soap with hand-washing education and developed a more resilient iodine to fortify salt against widespread deficiency, earning profits while solving systemic problems.

Sources of systemic problems include health, information, incentives and morale. Test with the five whys: ask "why?" at least five times until you reach the real cause; then find creative ways to solve or avoid it. Without understanding the roots, any solution is misdirected.

takeaways: Same problem as last year = systemic problem.
Warden's rings: leader, conversion process, infrastructure, population, action units.
IBM: incentives produced stability, not innovation; change the incentives.
Best Buy: biased information systems; diverse crowds forecast better.
Ask 'why?' five times to reach the systemic root.

terms.def: People, processes and things interacting as an integrated whole with structure, behavior and output.
A problem produced by how a system is designed, so it keeps recurring until the system changes.
Asking 'why?' at least five times to trace a problem to its systemic root cause.
Leader, conversion process, infrastructure, population and action units, from center outward.
Surowiecki's finding that diverse, nominally informed groups often predict better than a few experts.
U.S. Air Force strategist who revolutionized thinking about air power with a systems approach.
IBM chairman who diagnosed the incentive problem behind missed growth opportunities.

options: Incentives rewarding short-term profit over new businesses

quiz.why: Leader, then conversion process, infrastructure, population, action units.

quiz.why: It was off by less than 0.5%, later 99.9% accurate.

quiz.why: Fixing the systemic cause: impure drinking water.

options: You face the same problem as last year
quiz.why: Facing the same problem means you treated symptoms.

quiz.q: The five whys technique aims to find the truly systemic cause.
quiz.why: Keep asking until you reach the root.

case.title: The team that always misses the deadline
case.scenario: Every quarter, a product team pulls all-nighters the week before a release. Management responds each time with pizza, overtime pay and a 'lessons learned' meeting. Features are added to the release until two weeks before the deadline. Sales promises customers dates before engineering estimates the work, and the sales team's bonus depends on signed deals, not on delivered features.

questions.q: Run the five whys and identify the systemic problem.
questions.model: Why the all-nighters? Too much work at the end. Why? Features keep being added late. Why? Customers were promised features and dates. Why? Sales commits before engineering estimates. Why? Sales bonuses reward signed deals, not delivery. The root is an incentive and process system (like IBM's), not laziness or bad luck. Pizza and lessons-learned meetings treat the symptom.

questions.q: Design a systemic solution.
questions.model: Change incentives and process: part of the sales bonus tied to delivered and accepted features; no customer date without an engineering estimate; a feature freeze four weeks before release, with exceptions approved by one owner. Measure 'crunch hours' as a tracked metric so recurrence is visible.

lectures.title: Seize the Future with Scenario Analysis
lectures.hook: You can't predict the future, but you can rehearse several of them and pick moves that survive all.

sections.h: The paradox and the President's Daily Brief
sections.html: Sound decisions require knowing the future, yet it's unknowable. The President's Daily Brief gives the intelligence community's best estimate of the next 24 hours, to reduce uncertainty. In business, uncertainty means risk, and risk costs money. Chess shows the scale: one move ahead means 1,600 possible positions; two moves, 2.5 million. Scenario analysis is a mid-range answer: a menu of alternative futures built by asking "What if?" about key drivers and assembling the answers into plausible stories.

We already do this as training, rehearsal, standard operating procedures and contingency plans. Military, police and sports teams rehearse under conditions close to the real event: game-like practice, live-ammunition exercises, days-long stress evaluations. Businesses run war games to simulate crisis decisions, which also get leaders out of the boardroom where some options are taboo.

Herman Kahn developed scenarios about nuclear war at RAND in the 1950s. In the late 1960s Pierre Wack brought scenario planning to Royal Dutch Shell. If the future were 100% unknowable, planning would be useless, so separate the predetermineds (appear the same in every scenario) from the uncertainties (play out differently as the horizon extends).

1. Projects and decisions that are robust across different futures: measured against all scenarios, not the best one, and built to meet minimum expectations in each.
  2. Better thinking about the future: no single "official future."
  3. Richer interpretation of information than competitors have.

1. Identify the focal issue or decision (from your mission and objectives).
  2. Identify key factors in the local environment (customers, suppliers, competitors, success indicators).
  3. Identify driving forces in the macro environment (demographics, technology, industry growth).
  4. Rank factors and forces by impact and uncertainty to find the critical uncertainties.
  5. Select scenario logics: a two-by-two matrix of the main uncertainties, giving four possible worlds.
  6. Flesh out each scenario into a narrative, a story about the future.
  7. Determine each scenario's implications for the focal issue.
  8. Select leading indicators that reveal which future is unfolding.

Give each scenario a vivid name ("Crisis Mode," "Open-Market Dynamic").

Until 1965 Shell used "predict and control": a single-line forecast. Its scenarios first carried probabilities; the new approach made them equally plausible and focused on causality, not probability, to stretch executives' thinking. Of six oil-price scenarios in the early 1970s, the counterintuitive Crisis Scenario anticipated the 1973 embargo. Shell was better prepared than any competitor and later called tanker overcapacity and European petrochemicals correctly.

Personally: rehearse job interviews; for a speech, the predetermineds are the text and venue, the uncertainties are Q&A, the room and the equipment, so practice with a friend asking questions. Where uncertainty is unpredictable, prepare standard responses that work almost anywhere.

takeaways: Scenario analysis = several plausible stories about the future built from 'what if?'
Separate predetermineds from critical uncertainties (Wack).
Judge decisions by robustness across all scenarios, not the preferred one.
Process: focal issue, key factors, drivers, rank, 2x2 logics, narratives, implications, indicators.

case.title: Choosing where to live after graduation
case.scenario: Ana is graduating and deciding whether to sign a three-year apartment lease in Zurich. Two big uncertainties: whether she lands a job in Zurich or in another city, and whether remote work stays common in her field or fades. Predetermineds: she'll finish her degree in June, Zurich rents are high, and she wants to keep learning German.

questions.q: Build a 2x2 scenario matrix with named scenarios.
questions.model: Axes: job location (Zurich vs. elsewhere) and remote work (stays common vs. fades). 1) 'Home Base': Zurich job, remote common. 2) 'Daily Commuter': Zurich job, remote fades. 3) 'Remote Expat': job elsewhere, remote common, so she could live in Zurich anyway. 4) 'Forced Move': job elsewhere, remote fades, so she must relocate.

questions.q: What's a robust decision, and what leading indicators should she watch?
questions.model: A three-year lease performs badly in 'Forced Move.' Robust choice: a one-year lease or a sublet with an exit clause that works acceptably in all four. Leading indicators: where her interviews and offers come from, employer return-to-office announcements in her field, and job ads mentioning remote or hybrid.

lectures.title: The Correlation of Forces, Luck, and Culture
lectures.hook: Big impersonal forces push on you. Lucky people ride them; strategists also read culture.

sections.html: A Soviet Cold War term for calculating world power across military, political, economic, social, moral and revolutionary factors: a philosophy, a measuring method and a guide to action. The Soviets read the large impersonal forces, rode them, and tried to tilt them, which let a backward economy score notable successes against a richer U.S. For us it means the long-term environmental factors acting on a contest. We aren't at their mercy: like aikidō, we can position ourselves to redirect them. It combines all our environmental scans into a holistic, long-term view, so we can plan our response to curveballs in advance.

"Good luck" is largely a consistent behavior pattern that rides the correlation of forces; fighting it with brute or intellectual force tends to produce "bad luck." Max Gunther's five behaviors of lucky people:

  1. Many friendly contacts (networking).
  2. Attending to hunches: conclusions from real, if unconscious, data.
  3. Acting boldly (audentes fortuna juvat, "fortune favors the bold"): ready to accept opportunity, distinguishing boldness from rashness, not demanding certainty.
  4. The ratchet effect: getting out of bad situations fast. "If you are losing a tug-of-war with a tiger, give him the rope before he gets to your arm."
  5. The pessimism paradox: respecting Murphy's law and Mitchell's law ("Life is as slippery as a piece of soap..."); never surprised by the worst case.

These are positioning by principle: they don't guarantee victory but improve the odds.

Culture is a major current. Geert Hofstede (early 1970s) defined it as "the collective programming of the mind that distinguishes the members of one group or category of people from another." Its visible practices are symbols, heroes and rituals, which only become noticeable when you deal with another culture. Knowing cultural scores helps predict behavior, institutions and politics, and guards against stereotypes and mirror-imaging.

  • Power distance: how inequality in prestige, wealth and power is handled; shapes hierarchy. Russia 93, U.S. 40.
  • Uncertainty avoidance: how threatened people feel by the unknown; higher means more rule-driven. Greece 112, U.K. 35.
  • Individualism (vs. collectivism): individual or group rewards. Australia 90, Guatemala 6.
  • Masculinity (ego goals vs. social goals): Slovakia 110, Sweden 5.

No single dimension decides behavior; they combine into patterns of expectation. Firms often ignore culture because it's hard to quantify, which is exactly why understanding it is an advantage.

takeaways: Correlation of forces: read the big impersonal currents and ride or tilt them.

case.title: Leading a team across cultures
case.scenario: You're a project lead from a low power distance, individualist culture. You've just taken over a team in a country with high power distance, high uncertainty avoidance and strong collectivism. In your first week you invited 'everyone to challenge my ideas openly,' announced individual performance awards, and said the plan would be 'figured out as we go.' Engagement is low and nobody speaks in meetings.

questions.q: Explain the reaction using Hofstede's dimensions and the idea of mirror-imaging.
questions.model: You mirror-imaged your own culture. High power distance: openly challenging the boss feels inappropriate, so silence is expected. High uncertainty avoidance: 'figure it out as we go' creates anxiety; people want clear rules and plans. Collectivism: individual awards can embarrass people and hurt group harmony. Your behavior clashed on all three dimensions.

questions.q: What would you change, and which lucky behavior helps here?
questions.model: Give a clear plan and roles up front (uncertainty avoidance), collect input privately or through senior team members (power distance), and reward team achievements (collectivism). Gunther's behaviors: build many friendly contacts one-on-one (networking) and use the ratchet effect, dropping the failing approach quickly instead of insisting.

lectures.title: Strategic Thinking as a Way of Life
lectures.hook: Franklin, Churchill, Jobs and Winfrey: the strategic personality is curiosity, intent, boldness and follow-through.

sections.html: Uncertainty is everywhere. Success isn't predicting the future but preparing for it prudently, combining the course's tools and taking an active role in shaping your circumstances.

Franklin both visualized the future and crafted it, seizing and creating opportunities. At 21 he formed a discussion group that became the American Philosophical Society; he co-founded America's first public library and helped found what became the University of Pennsylvania. Curiosity plus a lust for life gave him legacies in science, politics, education, literature, military affairs and finance. His 13 principles were a blueprint; four of them (order, resolution, frugality, industry) suggest that you tackle uncertainty by building an island of certitude.

Expecting to die young like his father, Churchill moved with urgency: war correspondent at 21, riskiest military assignments, captured by the Boers, escaped. As First Lord of the Admiralty he fell after the Dardanelles failure in WWI and drew five truths for any operation:

  1. One must have full authority (the one he held most fiercely: never accept responsibility without power to act).
  2. A reasonable prospect of success.
  3. Greater interests are not compromised.
  4. All possible care and forethought in preparation.
  5. All vigor and determination in execution.

He spent the 1930s on the political periphery preparing a comeback, became prime minister on May 10, 1940, and led with a love of surprise and deception. He valued history as the guide to the future, and knew a good idea needs boldness, decisiveness and relentless follow-through.

Jobs exercised coup d'oeil relentlessly and reshaped six industries: personal computers, animated movies, music, phones, tablets and digital publishing. "Think Different" works as a mission statement for any strategy. Forced out of Apple in 1985, he bought Pixar and built NeXT. Back at Apple in the late 1990s, he refocused the company in a single meeting on four products (consumer and pro desktops and portables), then made Apple the hub for iPod, iTunes, iPhone and iPad. His traits: focus, strategic intent, drive, insight at the crucial moment, coordinated surprise, precise execution, detailed follow-through.

Winfrey turned curiosity and personal details into an enduring brand (like Franklin), voiced strategic intent in everyday battles (like Churchill), and shaped national tastes in books, health and politics (like Jobs). A strategic personality can thrive in any field, and the distance between us and the greatest strategists is rarely as big as we think.

Robert J. Hastings: "Regret and fear are twin thieves who would rob us of today." The strategic thinker mines the past for insight, lets the five-year goal shape today's moves, welcomes uncertainty and bends it, and refuses to be merely buffeted by events.

takeaways: Measure success by preparation, not prediction.

Jobs: radical focus (four products) and relentless execution.

case.title: Your one-year strategic plan
case.scenario: This is a capstone case about you. Choose one real goal you want to reach in the next 12 months (career, study, health, a project). Use the course's tools to plan it.

questions.q: State your mission and strategic intent for this goal, then list two measurable objectives.
questions.model: A strong answer has: a one-sentence mission (why this matters to you), a concrete, stretching strategic intent (Lecture 6), and two objectives that are clear, achievable and measurable with dates (Lecture 7). Weak answers are vague ('be better at X') or have no numbers or deadlines.

It closes options: it says what you'll stop doing.
